claim: Before designing a section, name the organisation's single primary conversion goal (leads, donations, signups) and justify every homepage module by how it moves that number.
why: A layout decision defended by its business outcome is a design argument; the same decision defended by taste is a preference. The former survives client scrutiny and reads as problem-solving.
when: Deciding what goes on a homepage or landing page for a client with a commercial or mission-driven objective.
fails: Sites with no conversion goal — documentation, reference, or internal tools — where forcing a persuasion frame degrades usability.

claim: For a services business seeking new clients, place social proof (testimonials, client logos, named results) on the homepage rather than burying it on a secondary page.
why: Trust is the blocking objection for a services buyer; deferring proof to a page most visitors never open leaves that objection unanswered at the moment of evaluation.
when: Agency, studio, consultancy, or freelancer sites where the visitor must decide whether to trust an unfamiliar provider.
fails: When there is no credible proof yet — thin or generic testimonials read as filler and cost more trust than the empty space would.

claim: For a nonprofit or mission organisation, lead with a concrete, time-bounded impact summary (what was accomplished in the last year, in specific numbers) instead of a mission statement.
why: Donors give against evidence of effectiveness, not against stated intent; specificity and recency are what convert sympathy into a gift.
when: Designing donation-driven pages where the ask is money from a visitor with no prior relationship.
fails: New or early-stage organisations with no track record, where vision and plan have to carry the page instead.

claim: Derive page order and section hierarchy from the sequence of questions a first-time visitor asks, not from the client's internal org chart or the order the content was handed over.
why: Layout is the highest-leverage UX decision available on a brochure site — it costs nothing extra to get right and determines whether a visitor reaches the ask.
when: Structuring any multi-section marketing site, especially with a fixed content set and no research budget.
fails: When real user research or analytics contradict the assumed question order — measured behaviour outranks the designer's model of it.

claim: Treat budget size as independent of problem-solving depth: apply the same goal-first reasoning to a small local client that you would to an enterprise engagement.
why: The constraint that blocks strategic work is usually the designer's own framing, not the client's spend; small projects still have a measurable objective to design against.
when: Working with small businesses, nonprofits, or early-career projects where the instinct is to just execute the visual brief.

claim: Present portfolio work as a problem-and-outcome narrative — stated goal, the decision made, the reasoning — rather than as a gallery of finished screens.
why: Screenshots only evidence visual output; if the offer is problem-solving, the presentation has to make the invisible reasoning visible or the buyer has no way to price it.
when: Building portfolio case studies, pitch decks, or proposals aimed at clients who buy business outcomes.
fails: Audiences hiring purely for execution craft — art direction, illustration — where visual fidelity is legitimately the product.

claim: Scope the initial design engagement so adjacent recurring services (search and conversion optimisation, content production, email, paid media, a maintenance retainer) can be attached later as separate line items.
why: The launched site is a starting point for measurable improvement, not a terminal deliverable; framing it that way converts one project into an ongoing relationship.
when: Proposing or pricing client work where the relationship could extend past launch.
fails: Bundling everything into one upfront quote, which inflates the entry price and obscures what the client is actually buying.

claim: Limit the top of a landing page or app screen to a single primary call to action; allow a second only if it serves a genuinely different user intent, and strip all other competing actions.
why: Attention is a fixed budget — every additional clickable element splits it, so the action you most want taken gets a smaller share.
when: Designing a header, hero, or any screen whose success is measured by whether users complete a specific action.
fails: Screens whose job is browsing or comparison — search results, product catalogues, dashboards, settings — where multiple parallel paths are the point.

claim: Treat the viewport as a budget you may underspend: leave regions deliberately empty rather than distributing elements to fill available area.
why: Emptiness around an element is what makes it read as the focal point; filling the canvas removes the contrast that creates hierarchy.
when: Composing any full-screen layout, especially on wide desktop viewports where extra horizontal space tempts you to add columns or decorative blocks.
fails: Content-dense interfaces where users expect density and would resent scrolling — data tables, email clients, IDEs.

claim: Decide the medium before you decide the density: for a portfolio shot, feed post, or concept image, maximise visual richness; for a shipping interface, optimise for a single clear next step.
why: The two artefacts are judged by different metrics — one is scored on whether a scrolling viewer stops, the other on whether a user succeeds at a task.
when: Any moment where you are reusing showcase-site or Instagram inspiration as the basis for real product UI.

claim: Audit a finished screen by counting its interactive and attention-grabbing elements; if a first-time visitor could not say within a second or two what the intended action is, delete elements until they could.
why: Density accumulates additively during design and is only visible as a problem when you deliberately step back and count.
when: Final review pass before handoff or launch.

claim: When you cannot cut a secondary action, demote it visually rather than deleting it — reduce it to a text link or ghost treatment so only one element carries full colour and weight.
why: Preserves necessary functionality while keeping a single dominant focal point in the visual hierarchy.
when: Screens with a legitimate secondary path, such as sign up alongside log in.
fails: When both actions genuinely serve equal-sized audiences and demoting one measurably suppresses it.

claim: Use major consumer products with famously sparse landing screens as the reference standard for focus, rather than the most-liked shots on design showcase sites.
why: Those products are tuned against real usage at scale, so their restraint reflects measured behaviour rather than aesthetic taste.
when: Choosing benchmarks or gathering inspiration for a product interface.
fails: Reference products serve one narrow task; copying their sparseness onto a genuinely multi-function tool leaves users unable to find features.

claim: Before adjusting individual margins, lay a column grid over each screen (e.g. three columns for wider/desktop-ish screens, two for narrower ones) and snap element edges to column boundaries.
why: A grid converts hundreds of arbitrary spacing decisions into a small set of shared alignment rules, so elements line up across sections without being eyeballed one at a time.
when: Redesigning a screen whose elements sit at inconsistent horizontal positions, or starting layout on a new screen.

claim: Allow specific elements to overhang or fall short of the grid when the composition still reads as balanced; do not force every object onto a column edge.
why: The grid is a scaffold for consistency, not a constraint to satisfy for its own sake — chasing perfect snapping can distort elements that were already working.
when: A few items resist the column structure while the overall page still reads as ordered.
fails: When breaks become frequent or unmotivated, at which point the grid stops communicating structure and the layout reads as unaligned again.

claim: In vertically stacked content, increase the gaps between items until whitespace itself does the grouping — related items close, unrelated blocks far apart.
why: Uniformly tight vertical spacing makes everything read as one undifferentiated mass; expanding the gaps lets proximity signal which elements belong together.
when: Stacked lists, sections, or content blocks that feel dense or hard to scan.

claim: Budget more vertical space on mobile than your desktop instinct suggests — deliberately overshoot your first estimate.
why: Narrow viewports compress content and reduce the surrounding emptiness, so spacing that felt generous on a wide canvas reads as cramped on a phone.
when: Adapting or designing any small-screen layout.

claim: Rebuild misaligned components like cards and chips with auto layout rather than hand-positioning their contents.
why: Auto layout makes padding and gaps declared values instead of dragged positions, so every instance of the component inherits identical spacing and stays correct as content changes.
when: Repeated components whose internal elements are visibly uneven between instances.

claim: Turn off vertical trim on text inside auto layout components so the spacing values you set are the spacing you actually get.
why: Default line-box behaviour adds invisible padding above and below glyphs, so a nominal gap renders larger than specified and optical spacing drifts from the numbers.
when: Tight components — chips, buttons, badges, card headers — where a few pixels of phantom padding are visible.

claim: Apply one spacing treatment across the entire product rather than tuning each screen in isolation.
why: Spacing reads as a system: identical components spaced differently on different screens make the interface feel assembled by different hands.
when: Any multi-screen product or design file with recurring component types.

claim: Derive a small set of repeated spacing values rather than typing a new number for each gap.
why: The demo sets the same kinds of gaps repeatedly across components, which only stays consistent if the values come from a limited, reusable set.
when: Setting padding and gap values across many components.

claim: Before adding a visible control, check whether the platform's native gesture already performs that action; on touch targets, drop carousel arrows and rely on swipe.
why: A control that duplicates an existing affordance adds visual weight without adding capability, so it is pure clutter.
when: Mobile or touch-first layouts with horizontally scrolling carousels, galleries, or card rows.
fails: Desktop or hover-driven layouts where no swipe gesture exists, and for keyboard or screen-reader users who need a focusable control; discoverability of a scrollable row can also collapse if nothing hints at more content.

claim: When you delete a competing control from a component, re-tune the remaining elements' emphasis rather than leaving them at their old contrast — usually by dimming them a step.
why: Emphasis is relative; removing one loud element makes whatever is left read louder than intended, so the visual hierarchy has to be rebalanced.
when: Any subtractive edit inside a component that still contains other interactive or accent elements.
fails: When the remaining element is the component's primary action — dimming it would bury the thing the user came for.

claim: Treat borders and strokes as decoration to justify, not a default: if a stroke isn't separating two things that would otherwise merge, remove it.
why: Most strokes exist out of habit; the underlying separation is usually already carried by spacing, background fill, or shadow, so the outline is redundant linework.
when: Cards, buttons, inputs, and containers that already sit on a distinguishable background.
fails: When the stroke is the only thing carrying separation or state (focus rings, disabled fields, low-contrast surfaces on the same fill), or where an outline is doing accessibility work.

claim: When you want to reduce an element's presence but can't delete it — for contrast, accessibility, or function — lower its opacity or contrast substantially instead of removing it.
why: Dimming preserves the element's function and any contrast obligation while stripping the visual noise that made it feel redundant.
when: Elements that are semantically necessary but visually overweight.
fails: When dimming pushes text or interactive elements below WCAG contrast minimums — reduction has a floor.

claim: Audit a screen by walking it element by element and asking of each one 'what does this do that nothing else here already does?' — delete anything with no unique answer.
why: Redundancy accumulates one reasonable addition at a time; only a deliberate pass over the finished screen catches it.
when: Reviewing a near-final layout, or cleaning up a design that feels busy without an obvious culprit.

claim: Allow deliberate exceptions: some technically redundant elements can stay if you have a reason, but name them as a judgement call rather than leaving them unexamined.
why: The rule is a lens for finding candidates, not an automatic delete; consistency, discoverability, or brand can outweigh strict minimalism.
when: When the same audit flags two similar elements but only one clearly deserves removal.
fails: When 'it's a judgement call' becomes cover for keeping everything — the default should still be removal.

claim: Harvest references at the level of the single detail, not the whole composition — if one element (a rule, a spacing move, a type pairing) is worth taking, save it even when the source image is low quality or badly cropped.
why: A reference's value is in the isolated idea you can reuse; overall polish of the source is irrelevant once you've extracted the move.
when: Building a mood board or reference set before starting layout work
fails: You copy the whole composition wholesale instead of the one idea — that's cloning, not referencing

claim: Set an explicit stopping point on reference/mood-board work: once further changes are ones a viewer could not notice, declare it done and move to the actual design.
why: Pre-design artefacts have sharply diminishing returns; time spent perfecting them is time not spent on the deliverable.
when: Any preparatory artefact — mood board, wireframe, style scratch file
fails: The 'invisible' tweaks are actually system decisions (type scale, spacing ramp, palette) that the real design will inherit — those are worth finishing

claim: Name the target context for the work before designing — a portfolio/showcase shot and a shipping product have different success criteria, and the choice governs how much UX rigour to invest.
why: Optimising for visual impact and optimising for task completion pull in different directions; being honest about which one you're doing prevents wasted effort and false claims about the result.
when: Starting a redesign, especially a self-directed or concept piece
fails: The showcase framing gets carried into real client or product work, where missing UX is a defect rather than a stylistic choice

claim: When a screen reads as 'stuff everywhere', fix structure before styling — establish the underlying layout grid or split first, and only then adjust colour, type, and imagery.
why: Visual polish applied over an unresolved arrangement doesn't register as improvement; the eye reads structure first.
when: Inheriting or auditing a cluttered existing screen

claim: Delete page furniture that doesn't serve the section's single job — social link rows, testimonial snippets, and site outlines usually don't belong in a hero and should be cut or relocated rather than arranged around.
why: Every retained element competes for the layout's attention budget; removing them is faster and more effective than trying to compose around them.
when: Reworking a hero or above-the-fold section that has accumulated secondary content
fails: The element carries real conversion or trust weight for that audience — then relocate it further down rather than deleting it outright

claim: Use an obvious placeholder image to unblock layout decisions and source the real asset in a later, separate pass.
why: Waiting for final imagery stalls structural work that doesn't depend on it; separating the two passes keeps momentum and prevents premature attachment to a stand-in.
when: Blocking out a layout where imagery occupies a large region
fails: The final image has a radically different aspect ratio, crop, or focal point from the placeholder, which can invalidate the layout you built around it

claim: For beauty and skincare heroes, default to an ultrawide two-column split — a full-bleed product or model image on one half, type and call-to-action on the other.
why: It's the established convention in the category, so it reads as credible immediately and gives the imagery enough area to carry the mood.
when: Designing a hero for a modern beauty, skincare, or lifestyle brand on wide desktop viewports
fails: Narrow or mobile viewports, where the split must collapse to stacked sections; also weak when the imagery is not strong enough to hold half the screen

claim: Rearrange borrowed ideas rather than transplanting them — take the mechanic (e.g. a thin dividing rule) and re-fit it to your own composition's proportions and spacing.
why: A detail that worked in the source depends on that source's scale and rhythm; unmodified transplants sit awkwardly.
when: Applying a saved reference detail to your own layout

claim: Set your desktop artboard to roughly 1920×1000, not 1920×1080 or taller — browser chrome and OS bars eat ~80-100px of vertical space on a standard non-curved monitor.
why: The design frame should match what a user can actually see without scrolling; designing at full panel height silently pushes real content below the fold.
when: Designing desktop web layouts intended for typical 1080p monitors in a maximised browser window.
fails: Ultrawide or curved gaming displays, laptops with shorter panels, and browser-chrome-free contexts (kiosk, fullscreen apps) all shift the usable height — measure the target rather than reusing 1000px blindly.

claim: Before refining any desktop layout, draw the true viewport rectangle over the canvas and check what falls outside it; treat everything below that line as scroll content, not hero content.
why: An overlay converts an abstract dimension into a visible cut, exposing which elements the user will never see on first load.
when: Any time a layout has been composed on a canvas taller than the real viewport.

claim: Distrust vertical spaciousness copied from portfolio shots — Dribbble-style presentations gain roughly 50% extra height that a real screen does not provide, so generous stacking there becomes a broken fold in production.
why: Portfolio work is optimised to be read as a static image at any size, not to survive a fixed viewport, so its spacing assumptions do not transfer.
when: Using dribbble/behance shots as reference or as the starting point for a buildable interface.
fails: Long-scroll marketing pages, where content below the fold is expected and the fold matters less than the first screen's hook.

claim: When a design overflows the viewport, compress vertical rhythm — section padding, stacked gaps, oversized hero blocks — rather than shrinking type or cropping content.
why: Vertical slack is usually the cheapest thing to give up; typography and content are load-bearing for legibility and meaning.
when: Adapting a tall composition down to a real desktop viewport.

claim: Delete decorative shapes that carry no informational or structural job — if removing an element doesn't degrade comprehension or hierarchy, it was noise.
why: Ornament without function consumes both space and attention in a layout already fighting for vertical room.
when: Cleanup passes on an inherited or reference design before restructuring.
fails: Where the shape is doing real work — establishing brand character, separating zones, or guiding the eye — in which case removal flattens the composition.

claim: Anchor a hero's image and copy to one side and group secondary imagery on the other, rather than distributing elements evenly across the width.
why: A committed left/right split gives the eye one entry point and a clear reading order instead of competing centres of gravity.
when: Composing a wide desktop hero with one primary message and supporting visuals.

claim: If the product has no logo, promote the wordmark: set the brand name in type and give it the prime top-left/header position rather than leaving the header nameless.
why: A typographic wordmark is a legitimate identity; an unbranded header reads as an unfinished template.
when: Redesigns where the source material shipped without a mark.

claim: Collapse low-frequency header actions — favourites, notifications, account extras — behind a single menu trigger to buy back horizontal space in the nav.
why: Header real estate is scarce; only actions used on most sessions justify a permanent slot.
when: Navigation bars carrying more than a handful of icons alongside branding and primary actions.
fails: Actions with high engagement value or state to communicate (unread counts, cart totals) lose their signal when hidden behind a menu.

claim: When you deliberately choose visual appeal over usability, say so out loud in the deliverable or handoff.
why: An unstated trade-off gets mistaken for a usability recommendation and shipped as one.
when: Concept work, portfolio pieces, and exploratory redesigns not bound by production constraints.

claim: Strip secondary nav items down to their minimum viable form — use a bare icon for universally recognised actions like cart, and plain text for account/sign-in — instead of giving every nav item a button treatment.
why: Multiple buttons in a header compete for attention and inflate the nav's visual weight; reserving button styling for the one primary action keeps the hierarchy readable.
when: Designing a header with several utility actions (cart, account, search) alongside primary navigation.
fails: The icon's meaning isn't universally understood, or the action is the page's main conversion goal and needs the emphasis of a filled button.

claim: It is legitimate to add a UI element purely to balance a composition — for example, inserting a search field to fill the gap left when other nav items were shrunk — provided the element is plausible for the product.
why: Compressing elements creates uneven negative space; a plausible filler restores symmetry without adding noise, and users rarely object to a feature that could reasonably exist.
when: A layout has become lopsided after reducing or removing elements, and a conventional, low-cost component fits the empty region.
fails: The added element implies functionality that doesn't exist or won't be built, which becomes a broken promise in the shipped product.

claim: Replace stand-in imagery with final high-quality assets before evaluating a layout as finished — poor photography will misrepresent whether the composition actually works.
why: Image quality dominates perceived quality in visual-product UI; judging spacing and hierarchy against bad photos produces unreliable conclusions.
when: Any e-commerce or product-led layout where photography is a primary visual element.

claim: When a card set has more items than the available width comfortably holds, convert the row into a horizontal slider rather than shrinking the cards or truncating the set.
why: Slider overflow preserves the card's designed proportions and keeps the full catalogue reachable, instead of trading legibility for a complete-looking row.
when: A fixed-width section needs to expose more items than fit at the card's intended size.
fails: Discoverability matters more than completeness — off-screen slider items get far less engagement, so critical items should not live past the fold of the track.

claim: Decide button placement within a card deliberately — treat which corner or edge the action sits in as a real design decision rather than a default, and iterate until it reads correctly against the card's imagery and text.
why: A card's action anchor sets the reading path and can collide with product photography or labels; the wrong corner makes the card feel unresolved even when everything else is correct.
when: Building repeating product or content cards that contain an inline action (add to cart, quick view).

claim: Add a small labelled chip (e.g. 'New arrivals') above a card group to name the set and give the section a light accent.
why: A chip functions as a compact section label that adds visual interest at a smaller weight than a full heading.
when: A card group needs categorisation or a bit of decorative punctuation without a heavy header.
fails: Overused — multiple chips per screen dilute the signal and read as clutter.

claim: Audit any text-over-image region for contrast as a discrete review step, and fix it at the image layer first — swap the photo, then apply a subtle dark overlay — before altering the type.
why: Photographic backgrounds have unpredictable local luminance; correcting the background preserves the intended typographic treatment instead of forcing heavier or recoloured type.
when: Hero sections or banners where headline copy sits directly on photography.
fails: The overlay must be pushed so dark that the product imagery becomes unreadable — at that point the image is simply wrong for text overlay and should be replaced or the text moved off it.

claim: Screen candidate background images against three explicit criteria — does it match the brand's mood, is the subject unobstructed in the region where text will sit, and is the lighting appropriate — and reject on any single failure.
why: Naming the failure modes turns an open-ended image search into a filter, which is what makes the search tractable at all.
when: Sourcing stock or library photography for a hero or full-bleed section.

claim: Use a subtle overlay — enough to drop the image's brightness but not enough to read as a scrim — when a chosen background image is only marginally too bright for overlaid text.
why: A light-touch adjustment preserves the photograph's character while buying back the contrast the headline needs.
when: The image is compositionally right but its luminance is slightly too high behind text.
fails: The image has high local contrast variation, where a uniform overlay fails and a gradient or localised treatment is needed instead.

claim: Justify each typeface by pointing to where it already appears in the brand system — logo, packaging, existing collateral — rather than by aesthetic preference alone.
why: Provenance in the brand makes a typographic choice defensible and keeps digital and physical touchpoints consistent.
when: Selecting or defending display type in a redesign for a brand that has existing assets.
fails: The brand typeface is technically unsuited to screen use at the sizes required, in which case a compatible substitute is preferable to consistency for its own sake.

claim: Build a hero or feature section as a fixed stack: headline, one line of supporting subtext, then a primary CTA paired with a secondary CTA — never two equal-weight buttons.
why: Subtext absorbs the explanation the headline can't carry, and ranking the two actions gives the eye one obvious next step while still offering an exit for users who aren't ready to convert.
when: Any section whose job is to move the user forward — product hero, feature block, pricing panel.
fails: Sections that are purely informational or decorative, where adding CTAs creates competing calls to action across the page.

claim: When a section needs a new element, reach first for a treatment already used elsewhere in the design rather than inventing a fresh one.
why: Repeating an established shape, button style, or motif makes the page read as one system and costs zero new design decisions.
when: Mid-composition, filling out later sections of a layout whose visual language is already set.
fails: The reused element carries a meaning that doesn't match the new context — reuse the form, not a mismatched semantic.

claim: Use a small circular icon-only button (a bare arrow, no label) as a low-weight tertiary link — e.g. 'browse the full range' — placed away from the primary CTA so it doesn't compete for the click.
why: It adds a visual anchor and an escape hatch to a broader catalogue without introducing a third block of text or a third competing button weight.
when: A composition feels visually unresolved in one corner and there is a genuine secondary destination it can point to.
fails: Shipping to production — an unlabelled arrow gives screen readers nothing and gives sighted users no idea of the destination; it needs an aria-label, tooltip, or adjacent text before it's usable.

claim: Decide upfront whether a piece is a portfolio/concept shot or a shipping product, and let that choice govern how far you push aesthetics past usability — then state the trade-off rather than pretending it isn't there.
why: Showcase work is judged on visual impact and can carry ambiguous, purely-decorative elements; production work is judged on whether people complete the task. Elements added because 'it just looks good' are the first thing to justify or cut when the piece ships.
when: Concept redesigns, dribbble-style shots, and any work presented as visual craft rather than a live interface.
fails: The concept is handed off as a build spec — decorative-only elements then get implemented as real, unlabelled, ambiguous controls.

claim: Trust a composition check at the end of each section: look at the finished block and ask what single element would improve the balance, then add exactly one thing and stop.
why: The 'this is good, but it'd be better with X' pass catches dead corners and unresolved weight that reading the spec never surfaces; capping it at one element keeps the pass from turning into clutter.
when: After the functional content of a section is complete and before moving to the next section.
fails: Applied repeatedly to the same section, or used to justify elements that add cognitive load in a task-critical flow.

claim: Use whitespace as the default separator between content groups; only add a divider line when the spacing alone leaves the grouping genuinely ambiguous.
why: Drawing a rule for every boundary is the classic slide-deck failure — it signals the designer didn't trust or didn't know how to use spacing, and the result reads as dated and over-decorated.
when: Separating sections, list items, cards, or content blocks in any layout.
fails: Dense information layouts — pricing tables, data grids, spec sheets — where space is genuinely constrained and a rule is the cheapest legible boundary.

claim: Don't restrict dividers to straight horizontal rules — let them curve, turn corners with a radius, or trace the edge of a region so they act as structural linework rather than repeated horizontal bars.
why: Curved and cornered rules read as an intentional graphic system rather than a default border, and they let the divider echo the shapes already in the layout.
when: When dividers are being used as a signature element of the visual identity rather than incidental separators.

claim: Treat divider styling as a signal of era and tone: hairline rules with generous space read modern and technical, while heavier or more frequent rules read editorial, rustic, or print-like — pick the weight and density to match the character you want.
why: The same device landed well on a deliberately rustic site and on a distinctly contemporary one, so the divider itself is neutral; the styling choices carry the period feel.
when: Choosing a divider treatment for a brand with a defined tone.

claim: Define one divider system — a single stroke weight, a single low-contrast colour, and a consistent inset from content — and reuse it everywhere instead of styling each rule locally.
why: The sites praised here read as cohesive because every line looks like part of the same drawn grid; mismatched rules make a page look assembled from fragments.
when: Any site using rules in more than two or three places.

claim: Audit each section that uses dividers in isolation: if the rules end up boxing content into a tight grid of compartments with little padding inside each cell, remove the rules and rebuild that section on spacing.
why: Even an otherwise well-executed divider system degenerates into a slide-deck table the moment cells get crowded, and one bad section undermines the whole page.
when: Reviewing multi-column or grid-like sections where rules run both horizontally and vertically.

claim: Check that the divider aesthetic actually matches the subject matter, not just the layout — a device that flatters an editorial or artisanal brand can feel borrowed on a product in a very different category.
why: The presenter's own hesitation was about fit between a linework style and a finance/crypto subject, even though the execution itself was competent.
when: Adopting a visual trend seen on a site from a different industry.

claim: When a layout renders every element at the same size, weight, and colour, treat it as a hierarchy failure and differentiate at least the primary element before adjusting anything else.
why: Uniform styling forces the reader to parse every field to find the one that matters, which is table behaviour rather than interface behaviour.
when: Information-dense cards, list rows, and summary panels where content is already logically ordered but visually flat.
fails: Genuine tabular data where column-wise comparison is the actual task and uniform styling aids scanning.

claim: Rank card content using only three levers — size, vertical position, and colour — before reaching for borders, shadows, or dividers.
why: These three carry almost all perceptual weight and keep the design from accumulating decorative structure that adds noise instead of order.
when: Establishing first-pass hierarchy on any content block.
fails: Layouts that additionally need grouping or separation between unrelated clusters, where containment cues do real work.

claim: Give each card a leading image when the content has any visual referent, and place it at the top of the composition.
why: An image injects colour into an otherwise monochrome block and gives the eye a fixed landmark, so scanning a list of cards becomes recognition rather than reading.
when: Repeating card lists — rides, orders, listings, bookings — where users scan many items to find one.
fails: Content with no meaningful image, where a generic placeholder adds weight without adding information.

claim: Place the single most important field at the top of the card and set it markedly larger and bolder than everything around it.
why: Equal treatment lets the primary field blend into adjacent metadata; both position and weight must agree for it to read as first.
when: Any card with one clear primary identifier and several supporting attributes.
fails: Cards with two genuinely co-equal primary fields, where forcing one to dominate misrepresents the content.

claim: Demote timestamps, dates, and other contextual metadata to a smaller size and position them beneath the primary field.
why: This content is confirmatory rather than identifying, so it should be available on a second pass rather than competing on the first.
when: Metadata that users check after they have already found the item they wanted.
fails: Interfaces where time is the primary sort key or the decision itself, such as a departures board or calendar agenda.

claim: Create hierarchy through relative contrast between elements, not by hitting absolute size or colour values — a heading is 'large' only relative to the body around it.
why: Perceptual rank is comparative; if every element is scaled up together, the ordering is unchanged and nothing is emphasised.
when: Any decision about type scale, weight, or colour emphasis within a single composition.
fails: Absolute constraints still bind — minimum legible sizes and contrast-ratio floors override purely relative reasoning.

claim: Set the key decision value (price, status, total) apart on a different axis from the primary field: top of the card, opposite horizontal alignment, and a distinct accent colour.
why: Differentiating it by alignment and hue rather than by size gives it its own rank without competing against the primary field for the same slot.
when: Cards where one value drives the user's choice and must be findable without reading the rest.
fails: Several values compete for the accent treatment, at which point the colour stops signalling importance.

claim: Express relationships between paired values — origin and destination, before and after, start and end — with icons and shared alignment instead of connective words.
why: A repeated icon column plus a common left edge encodes direction structurally, so the words 'from' and 'to' become redundant text the reader has to process.
when: Journey, transfer, range, and progression data inside a compact card.
fails: The icon vocabulary is ambiguous or unfamiliar, or an accessible text label is needed for screen readers.

claim: Accept that a given content set has several valid hierarchies; validate a layout against the heuristics — important content near the top, larger and more colourful reads as more important, use an image where one exists — rather than against a single canonical arrangement.
why: Hierarchy is a perceptual ordering with many satisfying configurations, so treating one composition as the correct answer invites pointless iteration.
when: Reviewing or iterating on layout options.
fails: An established design system or product convention already fixes the pattern, where consistency outranks fresh exploration.

claim: Set the vertical order of a card so that reading top to bottom matches descending importance.
why: Vertical position is read as rank by default, so fighting it with size alone leaves the two cues in conflict.
when: Vertically stacked card and list layouts.
fails: Right-aligned or corner-anchored elements that deliberately occupy their own reading zone, like the price in this example.

claim: Treat column grids and spacing scales as guidelines, not constraints — let bespoke sections such as landing-page heroes break the column structure when the composition calls for it.
why: Grids are a coordination tool, not a source of visual quality; enforcing them on one-off layouts adds rigidity without buying anything.
when: Designing custom, non-repeating sections where each element's placement is chosen deliberately.
fails: In systematic or multi-contributor interfaces, where off-grid placement compounds into inconsistency nobody can maintain.

claim: Reach for a column grid when the page is built from repeating units — card galleries, article listings, product tiles — and let it be optional elsewhere.
why: Repeating content needs a shared rule for how many items fit per row and where they wrap; unique content does not.
when: Any layout where the same component tiles across a region.

claim: Define the responsive contract by column count per breakpoint: 12 on desktop, 8 on tablet, 4 on mobile, and express component widths as spans so reflow is arithmetic rather than guesswork.
why: Fixed column counts per breakpoint make wrapping behaviour predictable and give every component a defined width at every screen size.
when: Building responsive grid-based layouts that must reflow across three or more breakpoints.

claim: Budget white space before you budget grid structure — if a section reads poorly, increase the gaps before adjusting alignment.
why: Breathing room does more for legibility and perceived quality than column alignment, and it's the cheaper fix.
when: Any dense or cramped-feeling section.

claim: Start a stacked section with one uniform gap — 32px is a workable default — between every sibling element, then reduce it only where two elements form a unit.
why: A single baseline gap gives a neutral, even rhythm; every deviation from it then carries meaning instead of being noise.
when: Vertically stacked content blocks: announcement bar, heading, subheading, CTA.
fails: When applied without exception, so tightly-related pairs float as far apart as unrelated ones and the grouping reads flat.

claim: Express grouping through proximity: pull related pairs (heading and its subtext, announcement and heading) to a smaller gap than the section baseline so the relationship is visible without a divider or box.
why: Relative distance is read as relatedness, making spacing itself a hierarchy mechanism rather than only a cosmetic one.
when: Any section containing more than two stacked elements with unequal relationships.

claim: Pick spacing values from a 4px scale (4, 8, 12, 16, 24, 32…) and choose sizes that stay divisible when halved.
why: Divisibility means you can always derive a valid tighter step, so the scale survives contact with real layouts instead of forcing arbitrary in-between values.
when: Establishing spacing tokens for any design system or multi-screen product.

claim: Justify the spacing scale on consistency, not beauty — 4pt multiples are not intrinsically more attractive, they just guarantee every designer and engineer lands on the same values.
why: Misattributing the benefit to aesthetics leads people to defend the grid in cases where it produces worse layouts.
when: Explaining or enforcing a spacing system to a team.

claim: Set a font size and a matching line height together for each text role — display heading, body subtext, button label — before you begin spacing the section.
why: Line height contributes to the visual gap between blocks, so spacing decisions made before type is settled will need redoing.
when: Composing any text-led section.

claim: Default to the conventional placement for structural elements — primary navigation along the top, content flowing top-to-bottom and left-to-right, primary CTA visually dominant and easy to spot — and only deviate when you can name the specific user benefit the deviation buys.
why: Users arrive with decades of accumulated pattern-matching from other sites; a layout that matches those expectations costs them no learning effort, while an unfamiliar one taxes every visitor to serve a preference that is usually the designer's, not theirs.
when: General-audience web and app interfaces, especially marketing pages, dashboards, and anything a user encounters for the first time with no onboarding.
fails: The deviation is genuinely justified by the use case — the narration explicitly allows breaking convention when it serves the user better. Also weaker for expert tools with repeat daily users, novel input paradigms, or non-LTR locales where the reading-order assumption inverts.

claim: Order content down the page and across the row in priority sequence: what matters most goes highest, and within a row, leftmost (in LTR contexts).
why: Reading flow follows the eye's trained scan path; placing the most important element off that path means it gets found late or not at all.
when: Deciding the vertical stacking order of sections and the horizontal order of items within a row or card group.
fails: Right-to-left languages reverse the horizontal axis; deliberately centred hero compositions and full-bleed focal images can override the row-order rule.

claim: Treat 'easy to add a new section later' and 'collapses cleanly at narrow widths' as evaluation criteria for a layout, not just afterthoughts — a layout that fails either test is a weaker layout even if it looks good at desktop width.
why: Conventional vertical stacking is inherently modular: sections are independent bands that can be inserted, reordered, or reflowed to a single column. Unconventional arrangements bind elements to specific positions, so every later addition forces a rethink and every breakpoint needs bespoke handling.
when: Choosing between two layout directions early, before committing to high-fidelity design.

claim: Locate your originality in the interaction layer and the feature set — motion, hover and transition detail, capabilities competitors lack — rather than in the macro layout skeleton.
why: The layout is what users navigate by, so novelty there costs them; the detail layer is what users notice and remember, so novelty there is pure gain. Splitting the two lets a design be both immediately usable and distinctive.
when: A design feels generic and there is pressure to make it stand out.
fails: Micro-interactions that delay or obstruct the task turn the differentiation layer into friction; decoration is not a substitute for a design that fails on structure.

claim: Before rearranging a standard component, ask whether the rearrangement is motivated by user benefit or by visual novelty, and discard it if the answer is novelty.
why: The chapter frames the moved search bar and re-arranged cards as things nothing prevents you from doing — the gate is not permission but justification.
when: Reviewing a layout decision that departs from what the same product category usually does.

claim: Before laying anything out, list the specific fields a screen must show, and derive that list from the decision the user is trying to make on that screen.
why: Content selection is upstream of layout; a grid or card only has value once you know what it is arranging.
when: Starting any content-driven screen — listings, feeds, search results, dashboards.

claim: On a browse or index screen, show only the fields the user needs to compare and shortlist items, and push everything else to the detail view opened on click.
why: Browsing is a scanning task; extra fields slow comparison, and the user has an obvious path to full detail when they want it.
when: Any list/grid of comparable items where a detail page exists.
fails: When there is no detail view to click through to, or when a decision genuinely cannot be made without a field — then it belongs in the summary.

claim: For a listing card, lead with the identifying and decision-driving facts — place, quality signal, cost — and demote descriptive prose to a single truncated line or drop it entirely.
why: These are the fields users filter on mentally; they should be readable in a glance without reading sentences.
when: Marketplace, travel, property, or product cards in a scannable collection.

claim: Treat any layout built on tidy sample data as unvalidated; re-test it with the longest, shortest, and messiest real values before considering it done.
why: Placeholder content is uniformly short and well-behaved, which hides every failure mode the real data will produce.
when: Reviewing any mockup where the text and images were authored by the designer.

claim: Give every text element an explicit overflow rule — usually truncate a title to one line with an ellipsis — rather than letting it wrap freely and push the layout.
why: Unbounded strings change element height, break card alignment in a grid, and shift everything below them.
when: Titles, names, locations, and any single-line label rendered from user or third-party data.
fails: When the full string is essential to the decision (legal names, addresses, error text) — then reserve space for wrapping or expose the full value on hover instead of clipping it.

claim: Never place an icon or label directly on top of a photograph; put it on a solid or scrimmed shape — a filled circle, pill, or gradient — so contrast is guaranteed regardless of the image behind it.
why: You do not control the imagery, so a bare icon that reads on a dark photo can vanish on a bright one.
when: Save, favourite, share, or badge controls overlaid on image content.

claim: When designing a component, enumerate its failure states as a checklist — longest string, empty field, brightest image, most items — and design a rule for each before handing off.
why: Anything left undefined gets decided by the implementation or the data, and the result is breakage you did not choose.
when: Any reusable component that renders dynamic content.

claim: Before adding a card or divider, try to achieve the same separation with whitespace alone; only introduce visible chrome when spacing genuinely fails to communicate the grouping.
why: Every border, fill, and rule is another visual element competing for attention, so a page with little actual content can still read as busy purely from its containers.
when: Any layout where content is being grouped into sections, panels, or list items.
fails: Container chrome is doing real work — an interactive card that needs a hit target or hover affordance, an elevated overlay, or a data table where rules aid row tracking across long horizontal scans.

claim: Use proximity as the primary grouping mechanism: set the gap between unrelated groups to roughly 2-3x the gap between items inside a group, so hierarchy is legible without any drawn boundary.
why: Human perception reads spatial distance as relatedness — close items are automatically parsed as one unit and far items as separate ones — so spacing communicates structure that borders only make explicit.
when: Structuring sections, form fields, list items, or any content that needs to read as distinct clusters.
fails: The available viewport is too tight for a meaningful spacing ratio, or groups sit side by side in columns where horizontal distance is fixed by the grid — there a subtle divider or background shift may be necessary.

claim: Budget for the fact that a card costs more space than its contents: padding, border, and inter-card gutter add fixed overhead on every instance, so multiply that overhead by the item count before committing to cards in a grid.
why: In dense multi-column layouts such as product grids the per-item chrome compounds, pushing content further apart and reducing how much a user sees per screen.
when: Repeating item grids and multi-column listings — e-commerce catalogues, search results, galleries.
fails: Item boundaries are ambiguous without chrome, e.g. items of wildly varying heights or with mixed media where a shared background is what separates one from the next.

claim: When removing containers, reallocate the reclaimed pixels into the gaps between groups rather than letting the layout collapse tighter — the removal only works if the whitespace grows to take over the separating job.
why: Deleting a border without increasing spacing just merges the groups; the border's separating function has to be transferred, not deleted.
when: Refactoring a boxed layout into an open one.

claim: Once boxes are removed, carry group identity with consistent styling of the remaining elements — give every icon in a set the same weight, size, fill treatment, and colour so shared appearance signals shared category.
why: Similarity is a second grouping cue that works alongside proximity, so it can replace the visual unity a container used to provide.
when: Icon sets, feature lists, and any group of parallel items whose relatedness was previously communicated by a shared container.

claim: Before finalising type scale and spacing, view the design at 100% on a device from the target class — a real monitor for desktop work, a real handset for mobile work — and revise sizes based on that view, not the canvas view.
why: Zoom level decouples the apparent size of an element from its physical size on the user's screen, so a canvas that looks balanced at 40% zoom ships type and gaps that are visibly oversized in use.
when: Any screen design where absolute sizes matter — body copy, headings, padding, touch targets — especially when working zoomed out to see a whole layout at once.
fails: Not addressed in the chapter; a real-device check does not substitute for testing across the range of viewports and pixel densities your users actually have, and one reference device can bias sizing toward that device.

claim: Mirror interactive prototypes onto a physical phone (e.g. via the Figma mobile app) rather than clicking through them in a desktop browser window.
why: Running the prototype on the hardware it targets exposes true scale, reach, and tap feel in a way a scaled desktop preview cannot.
when: Reviewing mobile app or mobile web prototypes before handoff or user testing.

claim: Subtract browser and system chrome from the frame height before deciding what counts as above the fold — design the safe content area, not the full artboard height.
why: The address bar, tab strip, and OS status bars occupy real pixels that the design tool's blank frame does not represent, so content placed near the bottom edge of the frame gets pushed out of first view.
when: Web designs on both mobile and desktop, and any layout where hero content or a call to action is meant to land in the initial viewport.
fails: Not addressed; mobile browser chrome is dynamic — it collapses on scroll — so treating a single fixed inset as gospel over-constrains the layout.

claim: Treat 'it looked right on the canvas' as an unreliable signal and build a real-viewing checkpoint into the workflow rather than relying on it as an occasional habit.
why: The distortion is systematic rather than occasional — it recurs for every designer who works zoomed out — so it needs a process step, not vigilance.
when: Any repeated design workflow that ends in handoff or publishing.

claim: Build a contained-card section by placing rounded-corner rectangles on a single flat dark ground rather than letting content sit directly on the page background.
why: The dark ground reads as one continuous plane, so the lighter cards separate from it by value alone and each becomes a discrete, scannable unit without needing borders or shadows.
when: Grouping several parallel content blocks (features, stats, product tiles) that should read as siblings inside one section.

claim: When cards are placed close together, lock the gutter to a single fixed value and apply it identically between every card and to the section padding, instead of eyeballing each gap.
why: Tight spacing removes the slack that hides inconsistency — at large gaps a few pixels of drift is invisible, at small gaps it reads immediately as sloppiness.
when: Any dense grid where cards nearly touch and the negative space between them is thin.

claim: Set the outer padding between the dark ground's edge and the cards to at least the gutter used between cards, so the group reads as inset rather than clipped.
why: If the frame padding is tighter than the internal gutters the cards look like they are overflowing the container instead of resting inside it.
when: Composing the card cluster inside its background plane.

claim: Choose one card treatment — same corner radius, same background fill, same padding — and reuse it in every section of the site rather than restyling per section.
why: Repeating a single container shape turns a one-off layout into a recognisable system, which is what makes a site feel designed rather than assembled.
when: You need visual cohesion across a multi-section marketing page or full site.
fails: Every section becomes an identical grid of equal cards, which flattens hierarchy — vary card size and span within the system rather than abandoning it.

claim: Prototype the section as a bare wireframe of grey boxes first and only then apply real content and styling.
why: Stripping the block to rectangles makes spacing and proportion errors visible while they are still cheap to fix, before imagery and copy distract from the structure.
when: Starting any new section layout in a design tool.

claim: Reuse the same card-on-dark block as a hero rather than designing a bespoke header.
why: The pattern carries enough visual weight to open a page, and reusing it means the header and the body share a language instead of competing.
when: The hero needs to present multiple parallel items (value props, previews) rather than a single headline and image.

claim: Reserve the photo-plus-statement band for a single line of copy that genuinely carries weight; if the sentence is filler, cut the section rather than filling it.
why: The whole section is one image and one line, so the line has to justify the vertical space it takes and the reader's full attention — there is nothing else on screen to carry it.
when: Adding a hero-adjacent statement band, mission line, or brand claim to a marketing page.
fails: Used for generic taglines or SEO filler, where the emptiness reads as a page with nothing to say instead of confident restraint.

claim: Place a full-bleed image band with short overlaid copy between two text-heavy sections to act as a visual interlude.
why: Consecutive dense text blocks fatigue the reader; a low-information image band gives the eye a rest and signals a change of subject without adding another heading.
when: Long scrolling marketing or editorial pages where several copy-dense sections run back to back.
fails: Stacked with other image bands or dropped into an already sparse page, where it stops functioning as contrast and just becomes more scroll.

claim: Constrain the band to a short, wide strip rather than a full-viewport-height hero.
why: The section is a spacer, not a destination — a shallow strip keeps it subordinate to the sections it separates and keeps the scroll moving.
when: Interstitial image sections in the middle of a page, below the fold.
fails: The same treatment at the top of the page, where a hero legitimately wants full height.

claim: Always put a gradient scrim between the photo and any text sitting on it — typically a dark-to-transparent gradient anchored to the edge the text sits against.
why: Photographic backgrounds have unpredictable local luminance, so text placed directly on them fails contrast in some regions no matter what colour it is; the gradient guarantees a consistent dark field under the type while leaving the rest of the image untouched.
when: Any time type is overlaid on photography or video.
fails: The gradient is pushed so strong or so far up the frame that the image is effectively muted to a flat colour field, at which point the photo stops earning its place.

claim: Choose the source image for this section knowing it will be cropped to an extreme wide aspect ratio, and check that the subject survives that crop.
why: A short, wide band discards most of a normally proportioned photo's vertical extent; images whose subject sits high or low in frame lose their content entirely, and images with fine detail read as noise at that scale.
when: Selecting or commissioning photography for banner and interlude bands.
fails: Portrait-oriented or subject-centred images where cropping to a strip destroys the composition — pick a different image rather than fight the crop.

claim: Keep the wireframe for this section deliberately near-empty: one image box, one text block, and nothing else.
why: The section's value comes from its restraint, so adding buttons, eyebrow labels, or supporting paragraphs would convert a rest stop back into a dense block.
when: Wireframing interlude and statement sections.
fails: The band is also expected to convert — if a CTA is genuinely required, use a different section pattern designed to carry one.

claim: Study several live implementations of a section pattern and rank them before designing your own version.
why: Comparing a strong example against a weaker one isolates which specific decisions — crop, copy length, band height — carry the quality, rather than copying a whole section blind.
when: Researching a section type before building it.

claim: Build the hero as a three-part vertical stack in this order: oversized headline, small nav links, then a large full-width image or video.
why: Putting the nav underneath the headline instead of above it makes the headline the first thing read and reframes the nav as a secondary caption, which lifts the headline's perceived importance.
when: Landing pages and portfolio/studio homepages where brand statement matters more than immediate wayfinding.
fails: Utility-heavy sites where users arrive to navigate rather than to be impressed — burying the nav below a screen-height headline costs them time.

claim: Set the hero headline at a display size on the order of 250-300px on desktop, and keep the nav links at normal UI size (roughly 14-16px), so the size ratio between them is at least 15:1.
why: The section reads as intentional because of the extreme discrepancy between the two type sizes; a moderate ratio just looks like an inconsistent scale.
when: A single short headline (one to four words) that can survive being set enormous.
fails: Long headlines or multi-line copy, which at that scale overflow the viewport and lose the single-glance impact.

claim: Use a condensed display typeface (Oswald or similar) for the oversized headline rather than the body typeface scaled up.
why: Condensed display faces are drawn for large sizes — tight letterfit and narrow widths let more characters fit at extreme scale without breaking lines.
when: Any headline set above roughly 100px.
fails: Display faces used below their intended size lose legibility and their tight spacing becomes cramped.

claim: Source hero imagery at resolution high enough to fill the full viewport width without visible softening — check the asset at 100% of its rendered display size before committing to it.
why: The layout deliberately blows the image up very large, so any resolution deficit that would be invisible in a small card becomes obvious pixelation.
when: Any full-bleed or near-full-bleed hero media.

claim: Pair the giant headline with equally giant media — a full-width image, slideshow, or video — rather than a small or inset image.
why: The two oversized elements reinforce each other; a modest image under a huge headline reads as unbalanced and drains the section's impact.
when: Hero sections using the oversized-type pattern.

claim: Wireframe this section in grey blocks before styling it, to confirm the size relationships and stacking order carry the composition on their own.
why: If the layout reads correctly with no typeface, colour, or photography, the impact comes from structure rather than from the assets covering for it.
when: Early layout exploration for any hero section.

claim: Rotate multiple images through the hero media slot as a slideshow when you have a body of work to show, instead of picking one static image.
why: It multiplies what the single largest element on the page communicates without adding any layout complexity.
when: Studio, agency, and portfolio homepages with a deep image library.
fails: Product or marketing pages where a rotating image competes with a single conversion message.

claim: When a section needs to show more images than fit on screen, keep one large hero image fixed as the visual anchor and put the overflow in a horizontally scrollable set beside it, rather than shrinking everything into a uniform grid.
why: The hero holds the visual weight and gives the section a focal point, while the scrollable set carries breadth without stealing hierarchy or forcing every image to be tiny.
when: Portfolio, product, gallery, or case-study sections with an image count that exceeds the visible area.
fails: There are only two or three images — the scroll affordance adds interaction cost for content that would fit in a static row.

claim: Pair the image set with a text block inside the same section instead of stacking a separate copy band above or below it.
why: Image-heavy sections often become pure decoration; embedding the copy in the layout lets the section carry a message and imagery in one visual unit.
when: Gallery or showcase sections that still need to explain what is being shown.

claim: Give any horizontally scrollable content set an explicit arrow or next control — do not rely on the scroll gesture alone to communicate that more content exists.
why: Off-canvas content is invisible; without a visible control users assume the visible images are all there is.
when: Any carousel, filmstrip, or overflow-scroll row on desktop.

claim: Add a position indicator (dot row or counter) alongside the scroll control so users can see how many items exist and where they are in the set.
why: An arrow says 'more exists' but not 'how much more'; without a count, users cannot judge whether scrolling is worth the effort or when they have reached the end.
when: Carousels with a finite, knowable number of items.
fails: Very long or unbounded sets, where a dot row becomes noise and a counter or progress bar reads better.

claim: For a more expressive version, scale each image up as it moves into the focal position and scale it back down as it exits, instead of scrolling items at a fixed size.
why: Size change tracks the user's scroll input and marks which item is currently 'the one', turning a flat filmstrip into a hierarchy that moves.
when: Brand-forward or editorial sites where a more crafted feel justifies the extra motion work.
fails: Content-dense or utility interfaces where per-item scaling costs performance and slows scanning.

claim: Choose the image orientation for a gallery layout before selecting the images, then source assets that already match it — do not crop mismatched images into the frame after the fact.
why: Heavy cropping to force a fit destroys composition and cuts subjects awkwardly; the layout's frame ratio is a sourcing constraint, not a post-processing step.
when: Any fixed-ratio image layout, especially mixed-orientation content sets.

claim: Build the layout as a wireframe first, mark the interactive controls explicitly in it, then render the high-fidelity version — and review the result for missing affordances before shipping.
why: The wireframe pass surfaces structure and control placement while it is still cheap to move things; the review pass catches affordances (like a position indicator) that only become obviously absent once the visual is real.
when: Designing any non-trivial interactive section.

claim: When a section must present many peer items but has limited vertical space, lay them out as a horizontally scrolling row of cards instead of stacking them into a tall grid.
why: A horizontal track lets a large volume of information occupy a fixed, shallow band of the page, keeping the rest of the scroll narrative intact.
when: Presenting a set of equivalent items — tours, plans, testimonials, features — where the user browses rather than compares all at once.
fails: The user needs to scan or compare every item simultaneously, in which case a grid that shows all items beats a track that hides most of them.

claim: Cap a horizontal card carousel at roughly 3 to 10 cards.
why: Below three there is nothing to navigate; past ten the click-through cost per item makes the pattern tedious and the user never reaches the end.
when: Choosing between a carousel and another layout for a known-size collection.
fails: The collection is large or open-ended — then switch to a grid, a filtered list, or paginated results rather than extending the track.

claim: Never make small arrow buttons the only way to advance a carousel; provide at least two navigation paths, such as a large primary advance control plus the small arrows.
why: Tiny hit targets are slow and error-prone, and a single navigation mechanism leaves users who miss it with no way through the content.
when: Any horizontally paginated section on desktop.

claim: Support direct mouse drag or swipe on the card track in addition to button controls.
why: Dragging matches how users already expect horizontal content to behave and removes the round-trip to a fixed control location.
when: Carousels on both touch and pointer devices.

claim: Place the small step arrows beneath the track and the large advance control above or beside it, so the two controls read as distinct in weight and priority rather than duplicating each other.
why: Differentiated size and position establish a clear primary action while keeping fine-grained stepping available without visual competition.
when: A carousel that offers both a primary and secondary navigation control.

claim: Design the carousel as a neutral structural wireframe first, then apply brand styling — the same track can serve a scheduling tool or a winery without structural change.
why: The pattern's value is in the layout mechanics; proving it in wireframe keeps the critique about usability rather than aesthetics.
when: Adapting a proven section pattern to a new brand or industry.

claim: Keep a carousel section visually restrained — a heading, the card track, and its controls, without additional competing elements in the same band.
why: The horizontal motion and the cards themselves already carry the section's complexity; extra elements make the band feel crowded.
when: Styling a card track inside an otherwise vertical page.

claim: Treat the bento grid's cell sizes and counts as provisional during wireframing; re-cut the grid after real content is written rather than forcing the content into the original boxes.
why: Each cell's proportions are dictated by what goes inside it — a short stat and a long feature explanation need different footprints — so a grid drawn before the content plan exists will misfit it.
when: Designing any mosaic-style section where multiple feature cards of differing weight share one grid.
fails: Late-stage work where the grid is already implemented in code and content must be edited to fit a locked layout instead.

claim: Split a row into more, narrower cells when the content naturally divides into more units than the wireframe allowed — e.g. move a two-box row to three boxes rather than cramming two ideas into one cell.
why: Cell count should follow the number of discrete ideas being communicated; one box per idea keeps each cell scannable.
when: Revising a bento wireframe after the copy and imagery for the section are decided.
fails: Subdividing past the point where each cell can hold a legible heading plus supporting element — narrow cells force cramped typography.

claim: Only choose a bento grid when you have enough substantive material — text, imagery, or both — to fill every cell; if cells would sit near-empty, use a simpler stacked or three-column section instead.
why: The bento's appeal is density: it presents many pieces of information compactly, so sparse cells read as unfinished rather than minimal.
when: Selecting a section layout early, before committing to a grid structure.

claim: You can adapt a reference layout by changing one structural variable — here, letting the grid span the full viewport width instead of sitting in a narrow centred container — while keeping its cell logic intact.
why: Borrowing the underlying grid relationships and altering the container width yields a distinct result without redesigning the pattern from scratch.
when: Working from a known reference implementation of a common pattern and wanting a differentiated outcome.
fails: Full-bleed grids on very wide displays, where cells stretch beyond comfortable reading measure and the density effect is lost.

claim: Start a bento section as a plain box wireframe with no content before styling anything, then iterate the box arrangement as content arrives.
why: The grid's structure is the hard part; resolving it in grey boxes is cheap, whereas rearranging finished, styled cells is expensive.
when: Beginning any multi-cell section design.

claim: Build knocked-out display type over imagery by placing an uppercase text layer over the image container and applying a boolean subtract, rather than faking it with a masked duplicate or a blend mode.
why: Subtract produces a single editable shape where the letterforms become true holes in the block, so the background shows through and the type stays live and repositionable.
when: Hero or feature sections in Figma where display type should read as a window cut into a photographic panel.
fails: Long or small text — subtract on body-size or multi-line paragraph type destroys legibility and turns the copy into noise.

claim: Use heavy uppercase type for cutout text, not lowercase or light weights.
why: The cut removes stroke mass and leaves the counters open to whatever is behind, so only thick, simple capital letterforms retain enough shape to be read.
when: Any subtractive or knocked-out type treatment over an image or texture.
fails: Delicate serifs, scripts, or thin weights, where the remaining strokes collapse against a busy backdrop.

claim: Choose the photograph for a cutout section by checking what sits in the region the cut will remove — typically the top corner — and reject any image whose subject, face, or focal point falls there.
why: The cutout permanently deletes that area of the image, so anything important in it is lost and the composition reads as an accident rather than a decision.
when: Selecting stock or client imagery for any layout where type or shapes are subtracted out of the picture.

claim: Select imagery whose aspect ratio and subject scale already suit the section's frame instead of cropping an ill-fitting image to fit.
why: A large image is the entire visual weight of this layout; if it has to be stretched or aggressively cropped to fill the block, the section loses its impact and the cutout has nothing coherent to sit against.
when: Image-dominant sections where a single photo occupies most of the viewport.

claim: Keep the cutout section's underlying structure to one image block plus one type element, and only then layer optional extras — a caption, a nav bar, buttons — on top.
why: The effect itself carries the visual interest, so a simple skeleton keeps it legible; the pattern accepts additions but does not need them to work.
when: Designing a section whose appeal comes from a single strong treatment rather than from compositional complexity.
fails: Adding so many knocked-out elements that the image is perforated and the underlying photo stops reading as a single picture.

claim: Apply the same subtract treatment to buttons and secondary shapes so they read as part of one cut plane rather than as elements floating over the image.
why: Consistency of the cut establishes it as the section's governing rule; a solid button over a cutout headline looks like two unrelated ideas.
when: Extending a cutout hero with interactive elements.
fails: Primary CTAs, where a knocked-out button may lose the contrast and affordance a user needs to recognise it as clickable.

claim: Sketch the section as a wireframe of plain blocks before applying the cutout, and confirm it holds up as a layout with no effect at all.
why: If the arrangement only works because of the trick, the section has no structure underneath it; the wireframe pass separates composition from treatment.
when: Adopting any visually striking trend into a real page.

claim: After a run of image-led sections, make at least one section text-only — remove the imagery rather than shrinking it — so the page has a change in rhythm and the copy gets the reader's full attention.
why: When every section carries a photo, the eye keeps landing on the images and the writing becomes wallpaper; dropping the image entirely removes the competition instead of just reducing it.
when: Long scrolling marketing or landing pages where several consecutive sections are photo-driven, and one section carries a message worth reading closely.
fails: The section's content is inherently visual (product shots, before/after, data) or the copy is too thin to justify the space it would occupy.

claim: Treat the empty area around a text block as an intentional element: leave it empty rather than filling it with a decorative image just because there is room.
why: Emptiness is what makes the text read as the section's subject; an image dropped in to fill space re-splits attention and undoes the reason for the layout.
when: Designing a section whose whole purpose is to foreground a written message.
fails: The void is so large that the section reads as an accidental gap or broken layout rather than a deliberate pause.

claim: Write or set body copy in a text-led section to run at least three lines at its display width; if the copy is shorter, either lengthen it or narrow the measure so it still forms a visible block.
why: One or two orphaned lines floating in a wide, open section read as an unfinished placeholder — the block needs enough mass to anchor the white space around it.
when: Supporting paragraph copy sitting under a headline in a spacious, image-free section.
fails: Deliberately terse formats — a standalone pull quote, a one-line tagline, or a caption — where brevity is the effect being sought.

claim: Use a wireframe to sell a layout idea when you cannot point to an existing example of it, then show the rendered version immediately after so the structure and the finish are both legible.
why: The wireframe isolates the spatial decision (what is present, what is deliberately absent) without the distraction of typefaces and colour; the render proves it survives contact with real content.
when: Presenting or documenting an unusual or under-used layout pattern to a client, a team, or an implementation agent.

claim: In an image-free section, open up the vertical padding beyond what the surrounding image-led sections use, so the removal of imagery reads as breathing room rather than as missing content.
why: Photographs supply visual mass; taking them out without adding space leaves the section looking short and depleted instead of calm.
when: A text-only section sitting between denser, photo-heavy sections on the same page.
fails: White space is added without a substantial enough text block to balance it, which just produces a sparse, empty-feeling section.

claim: When every competitor in a category opens with the same layout, keep the format your users expect but change one structural element inside it rather than inventing a new format.
why: The convention exists because it works for the content; novelty at the format level costs comprehension, novelty inside the format buys distinctiveness for free.
when: Designing a landing hero in a saturated category where the pattern is near-universal (automotive, SaaS, fashion).
fails: The convention itself is what's failing — e.g. the product doesn't photograph well or there is no single flagship item to feature.

claim: Filter image search results to large/high-resolution only before picking a hero photo, since anything below the viewport's pixel dimensions will visibly degrade once scaled to full-bleed.
why: A hero occupies the full viewport, so the image is upscaled rather than downscaled; artifacts that are invisible at thumbnail size become the first thing a visitor sees.
when: Sourcing any photograph that will be displayed at or near full-screen width.
fails: The asset sits in a small fixed container or is heavily blurred/overlaid, where a smaller file is preferable for load time.

claim: Choose a hero photograph where the subject occupies a modest portion of the frame; reject shots where the subject is tightly cropped or fills the canvas.
why: Full-bleed display magnifies the subject further, producing an aggressive, claustrophobic composition and leaving no negative space for headline, subhead, or CTA.
when: Selecting a photo for a full-viewport hero that must also carry type.
fails: The design intent is deliberate confrontation — a close-up product detail or portrait where the crop is the statement.

claim: Never place headline text over the focal point of a hero image; treat the subject's silhouette as an occupied zone and lay type into the empty regions around it.
