why: Overlapping type and subject makes both harder to read — the eye can't settle on either — and it reads as an accident rather than a decision.
when: Any hero, banner, or card that composites text on top of photography.
fails: The type is intentionally masked, knocked out, or layered behind the subject as a deliberate depth effect.

claim: Try the cheapest fix first — repositioning the text within the existing negative space — before reaching for a compositing technique.
why: Many overlap problems are solved by a small translation; escalating to masking when a nudge would do is wasted effort and adds fragility.
when: The image has a clear off-centre subject with usable empty area on one side.
fails: The subject spans the frame horizontally or the composition leaves no block of empty space large enough for the type at its required size.

claim: When a subject leaves no clean space for type, trace the subject's upper contour as a vector shape and subtract it from the text so the headline appears to pass behind the object.
why: It creates a layered depth cue that makes a flat photo feel three-dimensional, and it lets oversized type coexist with the subject instead of competing with it.
when: The hero image has a crisp, readable silhouette against a simple background — a vehicle against sky or road.
fails: The subject's edge is soft, busy, or low-contrast, or so much of the type is occluded that the words stop being legible; the remaining letterforms must still resolve into the word.

claim: Set headline type large enough that partial occlusion by the subject still leaves the word readable, and position the crossing point so it cuts through the middle of letterforms rather than swallowing whole words.
why: Legibility survives losing part of a glyph but not losing an entire character; readers reconstruct from partial letter shapes.
when: Using a subtract/mask technique to layer text behind an image subject.

claim: Put the logo in the top-left and the navigation across the top of the page; reserve vertical or side-rail navigation for cases with a specific justification.
why: Users scan for wayfinding in the conventional position first; an unconventional nav placement costs orientation time and also eats horizontal space the hero image needs.
when: Marketing and product sites with a standard top-of-funnel landing page.
fails: Apps and dashboards with many persistent destinations, where a vertical rail genuinely scales better than a horizontal bar.

claim: Collapse a long list of nav links into a smaller set — group or hide secondary items — so the header stays quiet against a full-bleed hero.
why: A dense header competes with the hero for attention and undercuts the impact the full-screen image was chosen for.
when: Redesigning a header that sits on top of a visually dominant hero.
fails: Hiding links that are primary conversion paths, where discoverability outweighs visual calm.

claim: When a hero image will carry an overlaid element (spec bar, badge, caption), choose or crop the image so the subject sits clear of that element's zone — pick the wider, zoomed-out shot rather than the dramatic tight crop.
why: The overlay is a fixed structural commitment; if the subject occupies the same band, you get collision and a compromised read of both. Image selection is downstream of layout, not the other way around.
when: Any hero or banner where text or a UI bar is composited over photography.
fails: If the overlay is confined to a solid or gradient band outside the image, or the image is a full-bleed background with generous dead space, the tighter crop can stay.

claim: Pull a product's key specifications out of a lower page section and into a persistent info bar directly beneath the hero.
why: The numbers are what a shopper is actually scanning for; making them reachable without scrolling shortens the path to the decision and frees the lower page for narrative content.
when: Product or vehicle pages where a small set of hard figures (range, speed, price, capacity) drives comparison.
fails: If the spec set is long or requires units and qualifiers, a bar flattens it into noise — keep it to three or four figures and link out to the full table.

claim: Use the info bar to seat a one-line teaser for a related sub-product, and let that teaser be the entry point for a dedicated section further down.
why: A short hook near the top creates demand for a section the user hasn't reached yet, and gives the page a reason to keep going.
when: When the page must sell a variant, package, or add-on alongside the main product.

claim: If the site header carries no call-to-action, the page body must contain an explicit CTA section — do not leave conversion to incidental links.
why: With no persistent action in the nav, there is no fallback route to conversion; a dedicated section becomes the only one.
when: Minimal or nav-only headers, common on brand-led marketing sites.
fails: Not applicable when the header already carries a sticky primary action — a second full section can then read as redundant pressure.

claim: Every image in a repeating card set must share one treatment — all cut-out on a common surface, or all full-bleed photographs. Never mix a backgrounded image with a transparent one in the same row.
why: Cards in a row are read as one system; a treatment mismatch breaks that reading and looks like an asset pipeline failure rather than a design choice.
when: Any grid or row of two or more parallel cards, tiles, or product entries.
fails: A deliberately asymmetric bento layout can vary treatment, but only when scale and position already signal that the tiles are not peers.

claim: Place card titles in dedicated space above the image rather than overlaying them on it, so legibility never depends on what the photograph happens to contain.
why: Overlaid text forces scrims, shadows, or careful cropping on every asset forever; lifting it out removes the contrast problem at the source and lets images be swapped freely.
when: Card and tile components where the imagery may change or be author-supplied.
fails: Editorial heroes with art-directed imagery can hold overlaid type, since the photo is chosen for the text and won't be replaced.

claim: Reserve the brightest accent colour for interaction states — reveal it on hover and focus rather than painting it into the resting layout.
why: A saturated colour used at rest dominates and desaturates its own meaning; held back for interaction, it stays legible as a signal and reads as restraint.
when: Brands with one high-chroma accent against an otherwise neutral palette.
fails: Hover-only accents are invisible on touch devices and to keyboard users unless the same treatment is bound to focus and the resting state is already understandable without it.

claim: Build the card hover as a small coordinated pair of changes — ease the image scale back and let the CTA button rise into view — rather than a single hard state flip.
why: Two linked movements read as one deliberate response to the cursor, and deferring the button keeps the resting card visually quiet.
when: Interactive cards on pointer devices where the action is secondary to the image.
fails: If the CTA is the primary conversion path, hiding it until hover removes it entirely from touch and scan-reading users.

claim: Do not apply a dark theme to an entire marketing page by default; choose it per section against the imagery and accent it must carry.
why: Blanket darkness flattens sectional rhythm and forces every photograph to fight its surround; the theme should serve the content, not the mood board.
when: Long-scroll marketing pages mixing photography, specs, and conversion blocks.
fails: Genuinely dark-native products — automotive configurators, media players — can sustain a page-wide dark treatment when the imagery is lit for it.

claim: Reuse a structural pattern you have already validated in earlier work as the skeleton for a new page, then adapt the content to it.
why: A known-good layout removes a round of structural guessing and lets the effort go into content fit and detail.
when: Redesigns under time pressure where the section's job is familiar.
fails: Reaching for the old pattern before checking whether the new content has the same shape produces a layout the content has to be bent to fit.

claim: Sanity-check a work-in-progress section against the live site it replaces, and treat 'already more professional than the original' as permission to move on rather than keep polishing.
why: The benchmark for a redesign is the incumbent, not perfection; naming the moment you clear it prevents over-investment in one section.
when: Redesign and critique work with a concrete existing comparison.
fails: A weak incumbent sets a low bar — clearing it is not the same as the section being good.

claim: Delete a section whose image, statistics, and message already appeared earlier in the page; repeating an asset lower down adds scroll length without adding information.
why: Scroll depth is a budget. A block the visitor has already parsed costs them time and dilutes the sections that do carry new information.
when: Auditing a long marketing page section by section, especially one assembled from a template where blocks were duplicated.
fails: When the repeat is a deliberate reinforcement at a decision point — e.g. restating the headline stat directly above the final CTA, where redundancy is the persuasion.

claim: When a feature section spreads a handful of items down a long vertical stretch, convert it to a horizontal slider so the whole set occupies roughly one viewport instead of several screens of scroll.
why: A slider trades vertical distance for horizontal navigation, keeping the feature set comparable at a glance and giving each image a consistent, contained frame.
when: Three or more parallel, equally-weighted feature items each paired with an image, on a page that is already long.
fails: When the items are not parallel in importance, or when the content must be crawlable and printable — slid-out panels hide content behind interaction.

claim: Cap the size ratio between a section heading and its supporting text; if the heading dwarfs the body enough that the two feel like different pages, shrink the heading rather than growing the body.
why: An extreme type-size jump reads as a template default rather than a considered hierarchy, and oversized display type forces the layout to spread out to accommodate it.
when: Feature or content sections where a display headline sits directly above short supporting copy.
fails: Hero sections and deliberate statement moments, where a large ratio is the point.

claim: Give two adjacent sections different layout structures even when their content types are identical; varying only the copy and images is not variety.
why: Identical structure back to back makes the second section feel like a scroll bug rather than new content, and the visitor stops reading.
when: Pages with several sibling content blocks — features, benefits, specs — authored from the same component.
fails: Systematic listings such as spec tables, pricing tiers, or product grids, where structural repetition is what makes items comparable.

claim: Pick the Bento cell arrangement from the aspect ratio of the assets you actually have; if the images are portrait, choose a grid built on tall cells rather than forcing vertical images into wide ones.
why: A Bento grid is only as good as the crops it produces — a wide cell fed a vertical image either letterboxes it or crops out the subject.
when: Building any tiled or Bento layout from a fixed set of existing photography.
fails: When art direction can be re-shot or the images are generous enough to crop both ways, in which case the layout can lead.

claim: Source a layout skeleton from a design gallery, then rebuild it around your own content instead of copying it cell for cell — expect to change the proportions substantially once real assets are in.
why: Gallery compositions are tuned to their original content; the structure transfers, the exact measurements rarely do.
when: Needing a fresh layout pattern for a section under time pressure.
fails: When the reference's distinctiveness is the brand's own signature — direct lifting becomes plagiarism rather than reference.

claim: Prefer image-forward tiles over accordion tabs for presenting product features; do not hide feature content behind a click that requires reading a label first.
why: Visitors scan visuals and skip collapsed text, so accordions bury the feature set behind an interaction most people never perform.
when: Consumer marketing pages selling a physical product with strong photography.
fails: Dense reference content — FAQs, spec sheets, documentation — where collapsing genuinely helps people find one item among many.

claim: Treat pure black as a decision, not a default, for section backgrounds on a premium page; test slightly-lifted near-blacks or tinted darks when flat black feels too heavy against the imagery.
why: Absolute black can read as harsh or cheap next to photography and removes the ability to layer darker elements on top of it.
when: Dark-themed sections carrying full-bleed or tiled product photography.
fails: OLED-targeted interfaces or designs where true black is a deliberate brand signature.

claim: If a feature is optional or only applies to some products in a range, do not give it a top-level section; surface it as a triggered detail (modal/lightbox) launched from the products it applies to.
why: Section-level placement implies the feature is universal and core; scoping it to its parent products communicates the actual relationship and keeps the page from padding out with content most visitors do not qualify for.
when: Product or marketing pages where a package, trim, or upgrade applies to a subset of the catalogue
fails: The add-on is a primary revenue driver or a key differentiator, in which case burying it behind a click suppresses discovery

claim: When a product variant has multiple eligible configurations, render one trigger button per configuration rather than a single generic 'learn more' — each button opens the detail view scoped to that configuration.
why: The button set doubles as a compatibility disclosure: the user learns which models qualify before opening anything.
when: An option, package, or spec is available on some SKUs but not others

claim: When setting text directly over a photograph, add a gradient scrim between the image and the type rather than relying on the photo's own tonal range.
why: Photos have unpredictable local contrast; a gradient guarantees a consistent dark (or light) field behind the text without flattening the whole image the way a solid overlay would.
when: Full-bleed or full-card imagery with overlaid headings, body copy, or captions
fails: The image is already uniformly dark or light in the text region, where an extra scrim only muddies it

claim: Every modal, lightbox, or overlay ships with a visible close control — treat the dismiss affordance as part of the component spec, not a finishing touch.
why: An overlay without an obvious exit traps the user; a click-outside-to-close behaviour is invisible and undiscoverable on its own.
when: Any layer that covers the page and interrupts the primary flow

claim: Keep modal content to a single idea: one image, a short block of copy, and nothing else. Do not nest secondary navigation or additional CTAs inside it.
why: The overlay is a detour from the main page; the faster it resolves, the less it costs the user to have opened it.
when: Detail overlays for supplementary product or feature information
fails: The modal is a task surface (checkout, configurator, form) where the interaction genuinely requires more controls

claim: Choose the CTA control by the next real action the user must take, not by default to a button — if the next step is location-dependent, use a search input (e.g. dealer/store finder) in the CTA slot.
why: A button can only send everyone to the same destination; the actual next step here is finding a nearby physical location, which requires user input to be useful.
when: Products where conversion happens offline or through a distributed network of locations
fails: The next step is genuinely single-destination (download, sign up, buy online), where a search field adds friction to a one-click action

claim: When reusing an established section layout for new content and it reads as flat, change two variables at once — flip the image/text side and shift the heading typeface — rather than redesigning the block from scratch.
why: Two targeted changes generate enough perceived difference to hold attention while keeping the underlying grid and spacing system intact.
when: Repeating a proven layout pattern across multiple content sections on one page
fails: Typeface changes accumulate across sections until the page has no consistent voice

claim: When three or more image/text blocks stack vertically with the same alignment, mirror the middle one so the composition zigzags instead of running as a single column edge.
why: Identical alignment down a page creates one long unbroken vertical edge that reads as a single undifferentiated slab; alternating sides gives each block its own entry point and paces the scroll.
when: Stacked alternating-content sections, particularly when a new block (like a newsletter form) is appended below existing ones
fails: Sections where strict alignment is the point — comparison tables, spec lists, pricing tiers — or on narrow viewports where everything collapses to one column anyway

claim: Re-audit alignment rhythm after appending a new section rather than only when designing it — adding a block can break a composition that worked before.
why: Layout variety is a property of the sequence, not of any individual section, so it can only be judged once the neighbours are in place.
when: Iteratively building long-scroll marketing pages

claim: Leave the footer as-is when its content is a dense, mandatory link inventory; spend redesign effort on sections where layout decisions actually change the outcome.
why: A high count of required links collapses the solution space to roughly one workable arrangement — grouped columns — so restyling it yields little and risks harming a wayfinding surface users already know how to read.
when: Redesigns of large sites with extensive legal, regional, and product link requirements in the footer
fails: The original footer is genuinely disorganised, unlabelled, or inaccessible — density is a constraint on layout, not an excuse for poor grouping

claim: Borrow interaction patterns from strong competitors in the same category instead of inventing new ones for routine problems.
why: Sector-mates have already trained the audience on the pattern, so adoption cost is near zero and the effort goes into content rather than teaching a novel mechanic.
when: Common UI problems — detail overlays, spec disclosure, configurators — in a mature product category
fails: The borrowed pattern is the competitor's actual differentiator, or it was designed around constraints your product does not share

claim: Include a customer/client logo strip as a standard section on a software or B2B product landing page, placed directly after the hero.
why: It is the most consistently repeated section across successful SaaS sites (41 of 50 in the audit), which signals it is doing reliable persuasive work rather than being decoration.
when: Marketing or landing pages for software, SaaS, or agency services where you have real customers or clients to name.
fails: Pre-launch products or projects with no genuine customers — fabricated or padded logo rows are dishonest and easy to disprove.

claim: Populate the logo strip with the most widely recognised names you legitimately have, rather than the largest count of logos.
why: The section works through instant recognition; an unknown mark contributes nothing and dilutes the recognisable ones sitting next to it.
when: Choosing which subset of a customer list to display when you have more logos than fit in one row.
fails: Audiences in a narrow vertical where niche-but-authoritative names carry more weight than generically famous consumer brands.

claim: Let the logo strip stand without explanatory copy beyond a short lead-in line — do not caption each logo or write a paragraph justifying it.
why: Audiences are already conditioned to read a row of brand marks as 'these companies use this product', so the inference happens with no context supplied.
when: Any social-proof logo band on a marketing page.
fails: When the relationship is ambiguous (investors vs. customers vs. integrations vs. press mentions) — then a label is required to avoid implying a claim you cannot support.

claim: Repeating the same logo set a second time further down a long page is acceptable and can reinforce trust at a later decision point.
why: An audited example did exactly this on a single page, implying reuse near a second conversion moment rather than treating the section as one-time-only.
when: Long-scroll landing pages with more than one call-to-action.
fails: Short pages, where the repeat lands within the same viewport region and reads as filler.

claim: Choose between two logo-strip layouts: a static evenly-spaced single row when the set is small and fits cleanly, or a continuous horizontal marquee when you want motion or have more logos than fit.
why: The static version is simpler and needs no motion code; the marquee reads as more polished and accommodates an overflowing set without shrinking each mark.
when: Implementing the section once logo selection is settled.
fails: Motion-sensitive contexts or when the marquee speed makes individual logos unreadable — the recognition benefit is lost if a viewer cannot resolve the mark.

claim: Treat the marquee as the upgrade path, not the default — reach for it when the page's overall production level warrants added polish.
why: The narration frames the static row as the personally preferred, sufficient baseline and the marquee as the 'fancy' escalation.
when: Deciding how much effort to spend on a supporting section.

claim: Terminate a horizontally-scrolling logo strip with an edge treatment that combines a colour gradient to the page background with a progressive (increasing-radius) blur, rather than a hard crop or a plain opacity fade.
why: A hard edge makes logos visibly get sliced mid-mark, which reads as a bug; a gradient alone still leaves sharp letterforms at low opacity. Adding blur that ramps with distance from the edge makes logos dissolve out of focus, so the strip feels infinite and the eye stays on the fully legible logos in the centre.
when: Any marquee, carousel, or overflow-scroll rail whose content bleeds past the container on one or both sides — client logo bands, avatar rows, card scrollers.
fails: The fade must resolve to a single flat background colour; over a photo, video, or busy gradient background the gradient mask will not match and the blur will smear the backdrop. Also unnecessary when the row fits fully inside the viewport with no overflow.

claim: Build the edge fade as a stack: mask/gradient for the alpha ramp, plus multiple stacked blur layers at increasing radii each masked to a narrower band, since a single blur filter cannot vary its radius across the element.
why: Progressive blur is not a native primitive; the perceived gradual defocus is produced by compositing several uniformly-blurred, differently-masked copies.
when: Implementing the described edge treatment in Figma or in CSS.
fails: On long, always-animating marquees the stacked blur layers are expensive to composite and can drop frames on low-end devices — cap the layer count or fall back to a plain gradient.

claim: When you want to position against named competitors, put the claim in a customer's mouth via a testimonial quote instead of asserting it in your own brand voice.
why: A first-person 'replace all of these tools' claim reads as aggressive and self-serving; the identical claim attributed to a real user reads as evidence. The page gets the comparison without paying the credibility cost.
when: Category-replacement or consolidation products whose value depends on the reader recognising the incumbent tools they already pay for.
fails: Brands with a deliberately blunt, oppositional identity can carry the direct version — and naming competitors at all backfires if they are larger or better-known than you, since you spend your page teaching the reader about alternatives.

claim: Treat competitor logos as a legitimate social-proof variant: a grid of tools you replace, laid out where a customer-logo band would normally sit.
why: It borrows the same visual grammar readers already parse as 'trusted names', but redirects the meaning from 'these people use us' to 'we absorb all of these'.
when: Consolidation pitches where the audience's current stack is the pain point.
fails: Products with no clear incumbent set, or where the named tools are complements rather than substitutes — the layout then just advertises your integrations as rivals.

claim: Default to the centred hero — centred eyebrow, headline, subhead, CTA pair, then a logo band — unless you have a specific reason not to; it is the layout the large majority of top-tier SaaS sites converge on.
why: Roughly two dozen widely-benchmarked products independently ship the same structure. That level of convergence means the pattern is repeatedly A/B-validated in the wild, so it is the low-risk starting point rather than a lack of imagination.
when: First-pass landing page or hero design, especially with no research budget and a broad top-of-funnel audience.
fails: Centred text stops working once copy runs past two or three lines — long headlines and multi-line subheads read better left-aligned, which is why a whole second tier of sites uses the left-aligned variant.

claim: Validate a layout choice by auditing a named sample of comparable products and counting adoption, rather than arguing from taste.
why: A countable roster of real sites is a defensible reason for a pattern in a design review; 'it looks better' is not.
when: Justifying structural decisions to stakeholders or choosing between competing layout directions.
fails: Popularity tracks what is safe and copied, not what converts for your specific audience — treat the count as a prior to test against, not as proof.

claim: Build the standard marketing section from exactly three ingredients: one oversized headline, one oversized supporting image, and a large amount of empty space around both — resist adding a fourth element.
why: The pattern's persuasive power comes from having a single focal point per screen; extra elements dilute the focus that makes it work.
when: Top-of-page or feature sections on a software product site where you need one idea to land per scroll.
fails: Content-dense contexts (pricing tables, docs, dashboards) where the visitor came to compare details rather than absorb one claim.

claim: Size the headline and image so that a single section roughly fills the viewport, forcing the visitor to scroll to see the next idea.
why: A screen that cannot show the next section creates a small, unconscious pull to keep scrolling — the visitor keeps consuming information without deciding to.
when: Long-scroll landing pages where progression through sections is the primary conversion mechanic.
fails: Pages where users need to scan and compare options quickly; forced scrolling then reads as padding and increases bounce.

claim: When a layout is industry-standard, differentiate at the detail level — typeface choice, image annotation, interactivity — rather than by restructuring the layout itself.
why: The structure is standard because it works; the cost of abandoning it is high, while small distinctive details buy recognition cheaply.
when: Designing in a category where a competitor scan shows everyone converging on the same section shapes.
fails: When the brand's whole positioning is being contrarian, or when the standard structure genuinely does not fit the content.

claim: Use a distinctive, non-default typeface as the primary differentiator when the layout itself is generic.
why: Type is the highest-surface-area brand signal in a text-and-image section — it colours every word without adding an element.
when: Headline-driven sections on a site whose layout matches competitors'.
fails: When the unusual face degrades legibility at large display sizes or lacks the weights and language coverage the product needs.

claim: Annotate the hero image with a small inline diagram, label, or callout that points at the part of the UI that matters.
why: A full-bleed product screenshot shows everything and therefore emphasises nothing; a lightweight annotation tells the eye where to land and doubles as a brand mark.
when: Hero or feature images that are dense product screenshots.
fails: When the annotation competes with the headline for attention or the screenshot is already simple enough to read unaided.

claim: Make the hero visual interactive when you want to out-differentiate competitors using the same static layout.
why: An interactive visual proves the product's behaviour rather than describing it, and it is the differentiator competitors are least likely to copy because it costs the most.
when: Products whose value is visible in a short, self-contained interaction.
fails: When the interaction is decorative, slows the page, or is not reachable by keyboard/touch — cost without payoff.

claim: Lay a very subtle gradient behind large flat sections instead of leaving the background a single solid colour.
why: Verification by toggling it off shows the section reads as bland and flat without it — the gradient adds depth at a level the visitor never consciously registers.
when: Sections with lots of empty space, where a flat background occupies most of the screen.
fails: When the gradient becomes visible as a gradient — banding, strong hue shifts, or reduced text contrast mean it has gone too far.

claim: Validate any subtle polish layer by toggling it off and comparing, rather than judging it while it is on.
why: Effects tuned to be imperceptible cannot be evaluated in place; the difference only becomes legible in the before/after switch.
when: Any low-opacity treatment — gradients, noise, shadows, background blurs.

claim: Use a purpose-built product visual (a dashboard or screen you designed) rather than stock imagery in the big-image slot.
why: The image carries half the section's weight; generic imagery wastes the largest piece of real estate on the page.
when: Software marketing sites where the product's interface is the proof.
fails: Pre-launch or infrastructure products with no meaningful UI to show.

claim: Give recurring section patterns your own internal names and reuse them as a vocabulary, since the industry has no standard terminology.
why: Named patterns become reusable components and make design decisions discussable across a team.
when: Building a library of marketing-page sections or a design system.

claim: To group a set of parallel content blocks (features, values, product pillars), draw them as cells of one continuous ruled grid — shared 1px borders running the full width and height of the section — instead of detaching them into individually shadowed or filled cards separated by gaps.
why: A shared line structure reads as one deliberate system and makes the section feel architected; free-floating cards read as loose objects placed in space and lose the relationship between items.
when: Marketing and product pages with 3–8 short, equally-weighted blurbs of roughly matching length.
fails: Items differ sharply in content volume or importance — a ruled grid forces visual equality, so a lead item that deserves emphasis gets flattened; also weak when cells must be individually clickable or reorderable, where card affordances communicate better.

claim: Anchor trend-driven layouts to a conventional, orthogonal column grid and express the trend only in surface details — a few degrees of card rotation, a border treatment, a hover state — rather than in the geometry itself.
why: Layouts built on ordinary columns are cheap and predictable to implement, so the design ships intact; exotic geometry gets negotiated away or approximated badly in build.
when: Any design handed to engineers on a normal timeline, especially in a component-based frontend.
fails: Brand-forward or award-targeting work where the unconventional structure is the whole point and build cost is accepted upfront.

claim: Reuse a single structural motif in at least two places on a page — e.g. run the same ruled-line treatment in the header and again in a mid-page section — so the page reads as one system rather than a stack of unrelated blocks.
why: Repetition of a structural device is what makes a page feel designed; a motif used once looks incidental.
when: Long scrolling landing pages assembled from multiple section types.
fails: Repeating it in every section — the motif stops being a signature and becomes monotony; leave sections between the repeats that use a different treatment.

claim: Layer motion onto the individual cells of a ruled grid — reveal on scroll, animated diagram or hover state inside the cell — keeping the grid lines themselves static.
why: The line structure is intentionally plain, so the interest budget has to be spent inside the cells; static lines also keep the section's skeleton legible while things move within it.
when: Once the static ruled layout is resolved and you have engineering capacity for per-cell interaction.
fails: The animations are elaborate enough to cost days of build time for a section users scroll past in seconds, or when motion runs simultaneously in every cell and creates competing focal points.

claim: Ship a deliberately reduced version of a trend pattern rather than a full-fidelity copy — the ruled grid works with plain type and no animation at all.
why: The structural idea, not the polish, carries the pattern; a stripped version is buildable immediately and still reads as current.
when: Small teams, early-stage products, or first passes where the animated version is out of scope.

claim: Put images or thumbnails inside expanded navigation menus next to the link labels, rather than relying on text links alone.
why: Users skim and largely do not read the copy that was written for them; a visual gives them something to recognise and act on faster than a label does.
when: Mega-menus or dropdown navs for products, categories, or content sections where the destinations are visually distinguishable.
fails: Destinations that look alike or have no meaningful imagery — generic stock art adds visual load without adding information; also risky in dense navs where images push the menu past the viewport.

claim: Delete divider lines between list rows, table rows, and sections by default; use vertical whitespace to create the separation instead.
why: A line is a second signal doing a job whitespace already does, so it adds ink and visual noise without adding information.
when: Any repeating list, table, settings panel, feed, or stacked content sections where items are already distinct blocks.
fails: The line is a deliberate stylistic device carrying the design's identity, or the layout genuinely cannot afford the vertical space.

claim: Size the gap between list items so the space between items is clearly larger than the space inside an item; if items still read as one block, increase the outer gap rather than adding a rule.
why: Proximity alone communicates grouping — separation is legible when the between-item gap visibly beats the internal line spacing, and a divider only becomes necessary once that gap has been starved.
when: Multi-line list items, cards, or rows containing a title plus supporting text.
fails: Vertical space is constrained enough that adequate gaps would push key content below the fold.

claim: When density is non-negotiable and rows must sit tight, separate them with a low-contrast alternating background fill rather than drawing a rule between every row.
why: A subtle fill separates rows using a whole-row surface change that the eye reads pre-attentively, without adding a hard high-contrast edge per boundary.
when: Dense data tables, long records lists, comparison grids where row height is capped.
fails: Contrast between the two row shades is strong enough to read as stripes and compete with content, or the alternation collides with row states like selected/hovered/error.

claim: Treat cramming a list tighter as a legibility cost, not just an aesthetic one — test any density decision by trying to scan the list and find one specific item.
why: The chapter proves the point by progressively tightening spacing until reading degrades, showing spacing is functional rather than decorative.
when: Any decision to reduce vertical rhythm to fit more content on screen.

claim: Before adding any new visual element — line, border, box, background, icon — check whether an existing element or whitespace already carries that meaning, and if so, don't add it.
why: Every element competes for attention; the design that communicates with the fewest parts is the clearest one.
when: General审 review of any interface, especially when a layout feels busy or cluttered.
fails: Removing the element also removes an actual affordance or state cue rather than a redundant one.

claim: Rank separation methods from lightest to heaviest — whitespace first, subtle background fill second, drawn line last — and only escalate when the lighter option has been tried and failed.
why: Each step up adds visual weight, so the cheapest sufficient signal is the correct one.
when: Choosing how to delineate any repeated or grouped content.
fails: A design system or accessibility requirement mandates explicit boundaries, e.g. high-contrast modes or dense financial tables where row tracking is safety-critical.

claim: To center a loading screen's contents in the viewport, set the wrapper to display:flex with align-items:center and justify-content:center rather than positioning children individually.
why: One flex context handles both axes at once, so the group stays centered as content size changes.
when: A single group of elements (logo + wordmark) needs to sit in the middle of a full-screen overlay or splash container.
fails: Multiple independent regions need separate placement, or content can exceed the viewport — centering then clips overflow at the top edge.

claim: When elements that should sit side by side are stacking vertically, add a flex container at the level that directly wraps them instead of changing the parent's flex-direction.
why: The outer flex container controls the group's position; a nested flex container controls the internal arrangement, so the two concerns stay separable.
when: A centered group contains a sub-group (icon + label) with its own axis requirement.
fails: Reaching for a nested container when a single flex level would do adds pointless DOM depth.

claim: Space a logo from its adjacent wordmark using the flex container's gap property, not margins on the children.
why: Gap lives with the layout that owns the relationship, so the spacing survives reordering or removing a child.
when: Two or more siblings sit on one flex row and need consistent separation.

claim: Commit a provisional spacing value (start at roughly 10px for an icon-to-text gap) and refine it visually rather than stalling on the exact number.
why: Optical spacing between a mark and type depends on the mark's silhouette and the type's size, so it can only be judged once rendered.
when: Early layout passes where structure matters more than final polish.
fails: The provisional value never gets revisited, or the project uses a spacing scale that provisional numbers should snap to.

claim: Constrain an inline or imported SVG's rendered size with CSS on the element; do not trust the asset's intrinsic dimensions.
why: Exported SVGs carry whatever canvas size the design tool used, which is usually far larger than the intended display size.
when: Dropping a logo or icon exported from a design tool into a layout.

claim: Target a single child asset either by descendant selector from its container or by adding a class directly to it — pick the class when the element may move or be reused.
why: Both produce the same result; the class decouples the style from the current DOM position.
when: Styling one image or icon inside a named wrapper.
fails: Descendant selectors break silently once the markup is restructured or a second image is added to the same container.

claim: Structure a navbar as three sibling containers — left nav group, centre logo/brand, right CTA — each a separate wrapper element, rather than a flat list of links.
why: Named sibling wrappers give you independent flex children you can align, space, and animate as units, which is what a symmetric nav with a centred brand requires.
when: Building a horizontal site header with a brand mark that must sit apart from the navigation links.
fails: Very narrow headers or mobile layouts where three side-by-side groups cannot fit and the pattern must collapse to a logo plus a menu trigger.

claim: Use two nesting levels for centring: an outer bar that is display:flex with justify-content:center to place the whole nav block in the viewport, then a separate inner container that lays out the individual nav sections.
why: Separating outer positioning from inner distribution means you can cap the inner container's width and change its internal spacing without touching how the bar sits on the page.
when: Full-bleed headers where the bar spans the screen but the nav content should be constrained and centred.
fails: Edge-to-edge navs that intentionally push a logo hard-left and actions hard-right — there the single-level space-between pattern is simpler.

claim: Give a nav CTA more visual weight than the text links by composing it as an icon with a short label stacked beneath it.
why: An icon-plus-label block occupies more area and reads as a distinct object, so the eye separates the primary action from the secondary link list without needing a different colour.
when: One nav item is the primary conversion target — join a community, sign up, open a chat server.
fails: Multiple nav items get the same treatment, which flattens the hierarchy back out and clutters the bar.

claim: Write the full semantic markup for a component before writing any of its CSS, and view the unstyled result once before styling.
why: The unstyled render exposes the raw document order and content hierarchy, so layout decisions respond to real structure rather than to placeholder boxes.
when: Building a self-contained UI component from scratch in plain HTML/CSS.

claim: Reference logo and icon assets by path from a dedicated assets location and treat them as swappable content, so the same container styling holds for any brand mark or icon you drop in.
why: Styling the container rather than the image keeps the layout stable when the asset is replaced or resized.
when: Nav slots that hold imagery — brand logos, social or platform icons.
fails: Assets with wildly different aspect ratios, which need explicit sizing constraints on the image itself.

claim: Style layout top-down: set the outermost wrapper's display and alignment first, then descend one nesting level at a time.
why: Each level's available space is defined by its parent, so styling a child before its parent means re-tuning the child once the parent changes.
when: Any nested flex or grid layout being built from scratch.

claim: For a horizontal bar with distinct left/right clusters, set the outer wrapper to `display:flex; justify-content:space-between; align-items:center` and give each cluster its own flex context.
why: space-between pushes clusters to the edges without manual margins or absolute positioning, and align-items:center keeps items of differing heights on a shared optical baseline regardless of the bar's height.
when: Header bars, toolbars, footers — any strip with two or three groups of items that should sit at opposite ends.
fails: With a single group, or when clusters must align to a specific grid column rather than the container edges — space-between will distribute leftover space unpredictably as the group count changes.

claim: Inside a nested cluster, use flex only for cross-axis alignment (`align-items:center`) and skip `justify-content` entirely — let the items sit at their natural start position.
why: The parent already handles horizontal distribution; adding justify-content at the child level would fight it and stretch the cluster's internal spacing.
when: Nested flex groups whose job is to hold a few icons or a logo plus label together as one unit.

claim: `max-width` alone does nothing to a block-level element that has no width to constrain — always pair it with `width:100%` (or a flex/grid sizing rule) so the element expands to fill and the max-width acts as the ceiling.
why: max-width is a cap, not a size. A block element already fills its parent, but once it's a flex item or otherwise shrink-to-fit, it sizes to content, so the cap never engages until you give it something to grow into.
when: Building a centered, width-limited content container inside a full-bleed bar or section.

claim: When you commit a magic number you haven't reasoned through yet, write it with an inline TODO comment naming it as provisional rather than leaving it silently in the stylesheet.
why: Placeholder values that look intentional survive to production; an explicit note preserves the distinction between a decided value and an unfinished one.
when: Any moment in a build where you need a value to keep moving but haven't derived it from the design.

claim: Separate adjacent icons with `gap` on the flex parent (starting around 10px for small icon clusters) rather than margins on the icons themselves.
why: gap applies spacing only between siblings, so no stray edge margin leaks out to offset the cluster from the bar's edge, and the spacing stays correct if items are added or removed.
when: Rows of icons, buttons, or nav links inside a flex container.

claim: Build layout outside-in: get the top-level distribution working, then descend one level and solve each group, then return for spacing refinements.
why: Sizing problems at an outer level cascade into every child, so tuning inner spacing before the container is constrained means redoing the work.
when: Composing any multi-level layout from scratch in the browser.

claim: When a hero's side-by-side split feels cramped, restack it vertically — headline, subhead, CTA, then visual below — so each element gets full-width room instead of competing for half the viewport.
why: A two-column hero forces both the copy and the visual into narrow columns; stacking gives each the full measure and lets whitespace do the separating.
when: Hero sections where the copy block and product visual are fighting for horizontal space, or where the split layout is the giveaway that a template was used.
fails: Not addressed; stacking pushes content below the fold, so it costs vertical real estate when the page has a lot to say above the fold.

claim: Replace stock photography in the hero with a screenshot of the actual product interface.
why: A real product view communicates what the thing is and matches the site's own visual treatment, where generic imagery communicates nothing and clashes with the surrounding design.
when: Any product or SaaS landing page hero currently using a purchased or generic photo.
fails: A raw, unframed screenshot with no focal treatment is only a partial fix — it informs but doesn't direct the eye anywhere.

claim: Let the product screenshot carry the page's colour, and desaturate the UI chrome around it — neutral white or near-white buttons rather than saturated brand-colour fills.
why: Colour sourced from real product imagery reads as evidence rather than decoration, and a neutral button stands out against a dark, colourful screenshot better than a coloured one competing with it.
when: Dark-mode pages built around a vivid product visual.
fails: Not addressed; on pages with no strong imagery, the buttons have to supply the colour themselves.

claim: Give the nav a two-tier hierarchy: render the primary action as an outlined or filled button, and set secondary links in plain text, optically balanced across the bar.
why: A flat nav where every item looks identical forces the visitor to read all of it to find the action; differentiating one item makes the intended path scannable.
when: Any header with a mix of navigational links and a conversion action.
fails: Hierarchy alone doesn't fix a nav that's simply too physically large — sizing is a separate correction.

claim: Reserve hover dropdowns for the nav items that lead to substantial sub-content; leave shallow links as direct jumps.
why: Which links expand becomes a signal of relative importance, adding a second layer of hierarchy without extra visual weight.
when: Multi-section sites where some nav entries front whole content areas and others point at single pages.

claim: Use identical label text for the header CTA and the hero CTA when they lead to the same destination — don't vary the wording for stylistic variety.
why: Matching labels tell the visitor these are one action shown twice; differing labels imply two different destinations and force them to guess which one they want.
when: Pages that repeat the primary conversion action in multiple positions.
fails: Not addressed; genuinely different destinations should keep distinct labels.

claim: Sequence sections so each one sets up the next, and treat the seams between them as designed transitions rather than hard cuts between unrelated blocks.
why: Without deliberate ordering a page reads as disconnected slabs stacked in whatever order they were built; a top-to-bottom argument keeps the visitor moving downward.
when: Long-scroll marketing pages assembled from modular sections.
fails: Correct ordering is necessary but not sufficient — abrupt visual joins between sections still break the flow even when the narrative order is right.

claim: Add a load-in entrance animation to the hero as the baseline motion pass, but treat it as a floor rather than the finished job.
why: A static page feels inert; a simple entrance introduces life, though generic fade-and-rise timing reads as cheap and marks the work as mid-tier.
when: Pages with no motion at all, where any movement is an improvement.
fails: Unconsidered easing and timing make motion actively signal low craft — worse than restraint in some cases.

claim: Cut the headline to a short, punchy line and keep the supporting subhead genuinely brief — one idea that extends the headline, not a paragraph restating it.
why: Long verbose subtext dilutes the headline it's meant to support and slows the read to the CTA.
when: Hero copy on any conversion-oriented page.

claim: Before designing, pull a reference set of real, shipped pages for the specific section you're building — heroes, CTAs, pricing — rather than starting from a blank canvas.
why: Working from what strong teams have actually shipped for that section type gives a concrete quality bar instead of guessing.
when: The start of any landing page project, and when stuck on a single section.

claim: When showing a product UI in a marketing section, crop into the single region that proves the point rather than displaying the full interface at reduced scale.
why: A whole-app screenshot forces the viewer to hunt for the relevant part; a crop makes the designer, not the viewer, decide what gets attention.
when: Hero and feature sections that embed dashboards, editors, or any dense product screen.
fails: Cropping away every chart and colourful element can drain the page's colour presence and make it read flatter than a wider shot would have.

claim: Frame the content column with thin vertical rules that run the full page height, and let the space outside them absorb extra viewport width.
why: The rules give the page a visible container and edge, so on ultrawide displays the layout reads as intentionally bounded rather than as content floating in an empty field.
when: Constrained-width marketing pages that must survive 1920px+ and ultrawide monitors.

claim: Replace uniform card rows with a bento grid where tiles differ in size according to how much content or emphasis each needs.
why: Equal-sized cards force every idea into the same footprint; varied tiles let heavier content breathe and create visual rhythm instead of repetition.
when: Feature or benefit sections where the items are not equally important or equally content-dense.

claim: Turn at least one static content group per page into a click-through component — tabs, a multi-select, or a slider — so the visitor manipulates something rather than only scrolling.
why: A single interactive module adds variety and signals a designer thinking about experience, not just composition.
when: Sections presenting three or more parallel options, use cases, or personas.

claim: Build type hierarchy from two variables at once — size step and colour/contrast step — rather than size alone.
why: Contrast reinforces the size relationship, so the reading order is unambiguous at a glance.
when: Section headers with supporting sub-lines or eyebrow text.
fails: Pushing both variables to the maximum makes the headline swallow the sub-line; the secondary line should still be comfortably readable, not visually discarded.

claim: Cut marketing copy down to short, punchy lines that describe what the product does overall, instead of paragraph-length feature explanations.
why: Shorter blocks let sections compress, which produces the tighter vertical rhythm associated with modern layouts.
when: Hero and top-of-page sections where the visitor is still deciding whether to keep reading.

claim: Shorten section heights as copy and layout tighten, so the page scrolls as a compact sequence rather than a series of tall, padded slabs.
why: Compactness is a direct consequence of shorter copy and denser grids; leaving the old spacing makes the tighter content look sparse.
when: After a copy-reduction or grid-densification pass.

claim: Add non-decorative brand elements — a trust badge, a customer logo row, a button that leads to a dedicated social-proof page — as deliberate parts of the layout.
why: These move the work from arranging interface elements to shaping how the product is perceived, which is where product design starts.
when: Landing pages that must build credibility for an unfamiliar product.

claim: Use a mega menu to expose the product's most important destinations in the header instead of a short flat nav.
why: The visible breadth itself communicates that there is depth worth exploring; a thin nav implies a thin product.
when: Products with genuinely multiple surfaces — features, use cases, docs, resources.

claim: Reintroduce the brand colour across the page, but keep the primary CTA as the most saturated, highest-contrast use of it, and pair that CTA with an icon.
why: Colour can recur without diluting the call to action as long as the CTA remains the strongest instance of the hue.
when: Pages where the accent colour appears in illustrations, badges, or product shots as well as in buttons.

claim: Audit total colour presence after any cropping or simplification pass, since removing visuals can silently strip the page of most of its colour.
why: Restraint at the component level compounds into an unintentionally monochrome page.
when: Late-stage refinement passes where elements are being cut for cleanliness.

claim: Attach subtle hover states to every substantial visual block — product shots, bento tiles, cards — not just to buttons and links.
why: Response on hover makes large static regions feel like part of a live product rather than pasted imagery.
when: Pointer-driven desktop layouts with large image or tile regions.

claim: Make carousels and sliders transition with continuous, eased motion rather than snapping between states.
why: Fluid transitions are the difference between a component that reads as engineered and one that reads as toggled.
when: Any multi-panel component the user advances manually.

claim: Design the seam between adjacent sections deliberately — let one section's subject introduce the next, and use a fade at the bottom of a visual to hand off to the following block.
why: Continuity across section boundaries is what makes a page read as one experience instead of stacked, unrelated modules.
when: Long-scroll landing pages with five or more distinct sections.

claim: Sequence a redesign by fixing visuals, layout, typography and motion first, and treat rich micro-interactions as the last layer to add.
why: Interaction detail reliably matures after the other principles; chasing it early on an unresolved layout wastes the effort.
when: Planning the order of work on a landing page refresh.

claim: Budget your polish across many small refinements rather than one signature element; audit each layer (imagery, layout, type, copy, colour, motion) for a one-notch improvement instead of adding a hero feature.
why: Perceived quality accumulates from consistency of care; a single impressive element sitting among sloppy details still reads as unfinished.
when: Taking an already-functional page from competent to premium.
fails: The page still has structural problems — hierarchy, unclear offer, broken flow — where detail work polishes the wrong thing.

claim: Crop and stage product screenshots to isolate the exact UI that proves the claim beside them, rather than dropping in a scaled-down full app view.
why: A zoomed whole-screen shot makes the reader hunt for the point; a purposeful crop makes the feature legible at a glance.
when: Any feature section pairing a claim with product imagery.
fails: The value of the product is the breadth of the whole interface, where an over-tight crop hides the scope.

claim: Break out of a uniformly rectangular grid: vary block sizes and let some content sit off the shared edges so the eye travels rather than scanning identical rows.
why: Strict alignment is the safe way to look organised, but repeated identical rows read as a template.
when: Feature grids, bento sections, and mid-page content once basic alignment discipline is already in place.
fails: Alignment discipline isn't there yet — asymmetry without an underlying grid reads as accidental, not composed.

claim: Loosen line-height and cap text measure so paragraph edges form a deliberate shape that funnels the eye toward the next element, instead of running text to the full container width.
why: Line width is a compositional tool, not just a readability setting — the ragged edge of a constrained block creates directional lines into adjacent content.
when: Hero subheads, section intros, and any supporting copy sitting next to a visual or CTA.
fails: Dense reference or documentation text, where consistent measure beats compositional shaping.

claim: Rewrite every feature line from what the product does to what the reader gets to do as a result — take the mechanic as given and state the outcome.
why: Description asks the reader to work out the value themselves; an outcome statement delivers the value directly and is worth more to them.
when: Feature headlines, section subheads, and bullet lists on a marketing page.
fails: Docs, pricing tables, and comparison pages where a buyer is checking whether a specific capability exists.

claim: Once imagery is curated and colour-controlled, pull one or two accent hues from it and repeat them across sections — glows, borders, icons, chart fills — so the page reads as one surface.
why: Colour can only be threaded consistently when the visuals feeding it are chosen rather than inherited; uncontrolled screenshots fight any palette you impose.
when: Pages where you control the art direction of every image and screenshot.
fails: Pages carrying third-party logos, user-uploaded content, or arbitrary screenshots whose colours you can't govern.

claim: Add a blur to state transitions and reveals rather than relying on opacity and movement alone.
why: Blur reads as depth and physicality, and it costs almost nothing to implement — one of the cheapest jumps in perceived quality available.
when: Section transitions, modal and menu reveals, carousel or tab changes.
fails: High-frequency or performance-sensitive animation, where blur is expensive to composite.

claim: When a persistent menu switches between panels, keep the container open and slide or swap its contents laterally instead of closing and reopening it.
why: Closing and reopening restarts the interaction and forces re-orientation; holding the container and moving the contents preserves continuity.
when: Mega menus, tabbed navigation, and sidebar panels with sibling views.
fails: Moving between genuinely unrelated destinations, where a clean close signals the context change correctly.

claim: Reveal secondary actions on hover or focus at their point of use instead of parking a permanent button under every item.
why: Always-visible controls add weight to every card and compete with the primary path; on-demand controls keep the resting layout quiet.
when: Repeated cards, logo walls, and list rows on pointer-driven layouts.
fails: Touch and keyboard contexts, where hover-only controls are unreachable — always pair with a focus-visible and touch-accessible path.

claim: Compose each section to the space it occupies so sections meet without dead gaps, giving the scroll continuous momentum instead of discrete stops.
why: Content sized for its container leaves no visual pause where the reader can decide they're done.
when: Full-page marketing layouts intended to be read top to bottom.
fails: Pages where each section is a separate decision point and a deliberate pause helps.

claim: Reach for craft in existing elements before commissioning custom illustration or 3D — refined motion, cropping, spacing, and copy get a page to top-tier without specialist assets.
why: The premium signal comes from execution quality, not asset expense, so the ceiling is reachable without a budget or an illustrator.
when: Small teams and solo builders deciding where to spend limited design effort.

claim: Choose footer structure from your own link count, not from the footer of a reference site; a multi-column link footer is a solution to having 20+ links, so only adopt it if you have 20+ links.
why: Large product sites have deep site maps that need columnar grouping. Importing that structure onto a site with six links produces mostly empty columns and a footer that looks broken rather than authoritative.
when: Designing a footer for a marketing site, portfolio, or small product site while using large industry-standard sites as visual reference.
fails: The site genuinely has a deep, multi-section site map — then the columnar footer is the correct pattern and collapsing it to one centred column would flatten a real hierarchy.

claim: For 3–5 footer links, use a single centred column: logo on top, the link row beneath it, social icons beneath that, all centred on the same axis.
why: With few items, a centred stack reads as a deliberate composition and gives the footer a clear focal axis, where a columnar grid would just distribute the same items into sparse, unbalanced groups.
when: The full footer navigation fits comfortably on one line at desktop width.
fails: Link count exceeds roughly five, at which point the centred row gets crowded and needs a different structure.

claim: Split the footer into two tiers: a centred identity/navigation block on top and a full-width utility bar underneath carrying copyright on the left and design credit on the right.
why: Legal and attribution text is lower-priority than navigation; pushing it to its own edge-aligned bar keeps it available without letting it compete with the centred content above.
when: Any footer carrying both navigation and boilerplate legal/credit text.

claim: Treat roughly five links as the threshold that decides footer layout — at or under it use the centred stack, above it design a different structure rather than compressing more links into the centred row.
why: The centred single-row pattern depends on the links fitting one comfortable line; forcing more in either wraps awkwardly or shrinks spacing until the row reads as a cramped list.
when: Deciding footer architecture at the start, before styling.

claim: Verify the finished footer in dark mode before considering it done.
why: The footer sits at the page's edge and often carries its own background fill, so contrast and separation from the page body can behave differently under an inverted theme.
when: Any project shipping both light and dark themes.

claim: Give the footer the same deliberate design pass as above-the-fold elements rather than treating it as leftover space.
why: Footers look bad mostly because they are assembled by default rather than designed; the fix is attention, not a trick.
when: Reviewing a page that is otherwise finished.

claim: Order footer elements by descending importance down the stack — brand mark, then navigation, then social links — so the eye lands on identity first.
why: The stack is read top to bottom; placing the logo above the links makes the footer restate who the site belongs to before offering where else to go.
when: Building a centred, single-column footer.

claim: Never validate an image-backed component against a single sample image; swap in at least one light, one dark, and one visually busy photo before calling the design done.
why: Overlaid controls are only as legible as the pixels behind them, and those pixels are content the designer does not control at runtime.
when: Any component where UI sits on top of user- or CMS-supplied imagery — carousels, hero banners, media cards, video players.

claim: Give every carousel a persistent indicator showing both the total number of slides and which one is currently active.
why: Without it there is no signal that more content exists or how much is left, so users cannot decide whether to keep swiping.
when: Any multi-slide carousel or gallery, including auto-advancing ones.

claim: When controls must overlay imagery, place them on a dedicated surface — a dark translucent pill with background blur — rather than setting them directly on the photo.
why: The surface guarantees a stable contrast floor independent of the image behind it, so legibility no longer depends on the photo.
when: Controls that need to float over media for space or aesthetic reasons.
fails: When the layout has room below the image; a solid non-overlapping control strip is simpler and more reliably legible than a blurred overlay.

claim: Offer the below-image control strip as the safe default and reserve the floating overlay for cases where the image should stay edge-to-edge.
why: Moving controls out of the image entirely removes the contrast problem instead of mitigating it.
when: Carousels inside content layouts where vertical space is available.
fails: Full-bleed heroes or fixed-height media tiles where a strip would eat the image.

claim: Group the arrows and the slide indicators into one control cluster instead of scattering arrows at the image edges and dots elsewhere.
why: A single cluster means one place to look and one target zone to reach, and the controls share the one blurred surface already built for contrast.
when: Carousels with both stepper arrows and position indicators.
fails: Very wide carousels where edge-anchored arrows genuinely aid reachability on large screens.

claim: If a carousel auto-advances, render the remaining time on the active indicator itself — a ring or bar that fills over the slide duration.
why: It converts an invisible timer into a visible countdown, so an unexpected slide change reads as scheduled rather than as the interface moving on its own.
when: Auto-playing carousels and story-style sequential media.
fails: Manually advanced carousels, where a progress ring implies a timer that does not exist.

claim: Build the progress timer by extending the active dot's own geometry into a ring rather than adding a separate progress bar element.
why: Reusing the indicator keeps the control cluster at one visual element instead of two, and ties the countdown directly to the slide it belongs to.
when: Dot-style indicators that need to express auto-advance timing.

claim: Verify the consolidated control cluster at mobile width before shipping — a single grouped pill should scale down without rearrangement.
why: Controls that were designed grouped survive narrow viewports; edge-pinned arrows and separated dots typically have to be redesigned for small screens.
when: Any responsive carousel.

claim: Make the primary header CTA an input-like action when the product experience starts with user text, and redirect to authentication only after the user begins the action.
why: Beginning with a prompt gets people invested in the task before the login requirement appears, which can make completion more likely than a passive login button.
when: The core product interaction is typing a query, request, or prompt and authentication is needed to continue.
fails: It can mislead users if typed content will be lost, the action cannot actually be continued after login, or the header’s main job is account access rather than task initiation.

claim: Use a concise, high-impact headline to establish the product proposition before adding supporting detail.
why: A punchy statement gives the header a clear focal message and borrows the immediate clarity of effective product-marketing pages.
when: A landing-page hero needs to communicate a single positioning claim quickly.
fails: It becomes weak when the claim is vague, unprovable, or hides essential qualification behind marketing language.

claim: In a clean branded interface, apply brand colour selectively rather than forcing every logo colour into the hero.
why: The direct multicolour treatment was judged visually off; a white-backed logo and a separate product symbol preserved recognition with less visual conflict.
when: A strongly coloured brand is being placed in a restrained or dark hero composition.
fails: It may underuse necessary brand cues in contexts where brand colour is the primary means of recognition or differentiation.

claim: Avoid generic decorative shapes when they compete with a deliberately minimal visual system.
why: The tested background shapes made the header feel messy relative to the clean Google-like direction.
when: The layout already has strong type, brand marks, and a clear primary interaction.
fails: Decorative forms can work when they are part of the established brand system or support hierarchy without adding noise.

claim: Use product-native motion as hero decoration when possible, such as a loading or thinking state that communicates what the AI does.
why: A chatbot loading treatment is more attention-grabbing and more meaningful than arbitrary background ornament because it makes the interface feel active.
when: The product has recognizable states or interactions that can be safely shown as ambient motion.
fails: It distracts when the motion is too prominent, suggests a wait state users cannot act on, or reduces readability and performance.

claim: Choose a section layout that has enough visual and spatial capacity for all required content; replace an attractive reference pattern if it forces important material out.
why: A layout that cannot carry the needed information produces an incomplete section, regardless of how good the reference looks.
when: Designing a content-rich product feature section.

claim: Establish hierarchy and visual appeal with the static layout before relying on motion effects.
why: The chapter demonstrates that a well-composed section already feels effective before any animation is applied.
when: Designing marketing-page sections with planned motion or hover interactions.

claim: When separate landing pages communicate substantially the same offer, merge them into one focused section organized around the few factors users need to compare.
why: Consolidation removes redundant destinations and makes pricing, capability level, and supported file inputs easier to scan.
when: Multiple product tiers or pages overlap for the same audience.
fails: Distinct offers require separate audiences, conversion paths, or decision information.

claim: Use interactive cards to compact detail: on hover, enlarge and soften the visual background while revealing explanatory copy.
why: The interaction preserves a concise default state but provides richer information on demand.
when: A card grid needs to communicate several product benefits without exposing all copy at once.
fails: Critical information must remain visible for touch users, accessibility, or immediate comparison.

claim: Place conversion actions in the context of the relevant option card when users are choosing among offers.
why: Embedding the purchase call to action in a card connects the action directly to its associated product choice.
when: A section presents multiple plans, capabilities, or upgrade paths.

claim: Demote niche content to a small secondary control instead of giving it equal visual weight with the primary audience's needs.
why: Enterprise material is described as irrelevant to most visitors, so prominent placement would distract from the common path.
when: A general-audience page also needs to retain access to a specialized offering.
fails: The specialized offering is a primary conversion goal or its audience needs immediate visibility.

claim: Use an element that extends beyond the viewport or section container to make an otherwise simple content layout feel less boxed-in.
why: Breaking the container edge creates visual energy and makes the exploration area feel more expansive.
when: A product-marketing section needs a memorable layout without adding dense content.
fails: The overflow obscures essential content or causes poor horizontal behavior on small screens.

claim: Simplify generated decorative color into a restrained brand color system when the initial treatment competes with the interface.
why: A recognizable primary color and a subdued supporting background keep the section cohesive and easier to scan.
when: AI-generated or stock visual assets introduce gradients or colors that feel generic or overly busy.
fails: A deliberately expressive campaign requires broad, high-contrast color variation.

claim: Give hoverable cards or controls a visible state change, such as a branded gradient stroke, to communicate interactivity while preserving a calm default appearance.
why: The interaction state adds color and feedback only when needed instead of making the resting layout noisy.
when: Interactive tiles, plans, or navigation items need clearer affordance.
fails: The stroke has insufficient contrast, distracts from content, or is the only way keyboard users receive focus feedback.

claim: For software and hardware interfaces, choose clean, simple interface icons rather than highly decorative iconography.
why: Minimal icons better match product UI and avoid visual clutter.
when: Sourcing icons for controls, feature cards, or technical product messaging.
fails: The icon must carry a strong brand, cultural, or editorial meaning that simple interface symbols cannot convey.

claim: Include a dedicated privacy and security message when the product handles user data.
why: Data-related products need explicit trust signals alongside benefit-focused marketing.
when: A product collects, processes, stores, or makes recommendations from user information.

claim: Select trust iconography that fits the product's own visual language instead of copying a competitor's familiar symbol.
why: A shield can express protection while feeling more aligned with the intended brand than a lock.
when: Designing visual cues for security, privacy, or reliability claims.
fails: Established platform conventions or user research make another symbol substantially clearer.

claim: When a literal illustration feels weak, iterate toward a coherent geometric visual system—such as grids, isometric forms, and repeated circles—rather than merely adding isolated decoration.
why: A shared spatial language gives the security module more depth and intentionality.
when: An abstract marketing illustration lacks distinctiveness or visual structure.
fails: The added geometry reduces clarity, accessibility, or performance.

claim: End an exploration or feature sequence with a direct CTA that asks users to try the product.
why: After presenting possibilities and trust signals, the interface should provide an immediate conversion path.
when: A marketing page has completed its value proposition and reassurance narrative.
fails: Users still need pricing, eligibility, or setup information before they can act confidently.

claim: Iterate through multiple layout variants before committing when the primary CTA composition does not feel visually balanced.
why: Comparing alternatives exposes problems with hierarchy, spacing, and interaction placement that are hard to predict in a first draft.
when: Designing a prominent landing-page section with several competing elements, such as prompt suggestions and an input control.
fails: The variants do not test a clear hypothesis or cannot be evaluated against user and product goals.

claim: Make the main action the visual center of a CTA section; demote supporting or decorative prompt content to the periphery.
why: A centered input gives users an obvious starting point, while side content can add atmosphere without competing for attention.
when: The page's main conversion action is entering a query, prompt, or other short input.
fails: The supporting cards are necessary choices users must read and compare before acting.

claim: Use gradients and peripheral placement to reduce the visual weight of decorative elements around a focal control.
why: They preserve visual richness while maintaining a clear hierarchy toward the primary interaction.
when: Supplementary cards or examples add character but are not essential to task completion.
fails: Low contrast makes required content inaccessible or obscures interactive affordances.

claim: Vary section layouts across a landing page when repeating an existing pattern would make later content feel redundant.
why: A distinct blog presentation helps preserve rhythm and gives each content type its own role.
when: Multiple sections would otherwise use the same card-grid or editorial arrangement.
fails: Consistency is more important than variety, such as in a tightly standardized product system.

claim: Reuse proven visual patterns from related parts of the experience for global chrome such as headers and footers, adapting branding as needed.
why: Repetition of navigation structure creates cohesion and reduces unnecessary design invention.
when: Building global site navigation or a footer for a branded product landing page.
fails: The borrowed pattern conflicts with the product's information architecture, accessibility requirements, or brand rules.

claim: Compose each UI section so its visual hierarchy directs attention along a deliberate path instead of making multiple elements fight for equal prominence.
why: A captivating design draws people in and guides their eye, whereas competing focal points create chaos and weaken the experience.
when: Designing content-heavy sections, landing pages, or any interface where users need to notice information in a preferred order.
fails: null
