claim: Use structural order, repeated visual rhythm, and a small amount of surprise together to make a section feel engaging without becoming noisy.
why: The chapter presents these as the ingredients behind an interface that feels right rather than merely looking pleasant.
when: Creating expressive marketing or editorial UI sections that need both clarity and memorability.
fails: Surprise becomes counterproductive when it overwhelms the hierarchy or introduces too many competing accents.

claim: Organize sections around a simple grid and generous whitespace, prioritizing a few clear content groups over many competing components.
why: Fewer visual units and more room around them make the page easier to scan and give the user a clear route through the content.
when: Designing marketing sections, product pages, or landing-page heroes that need to communicate quickly.
fails: A dense information task genuinely requires simultaneous comparison or controls; in that case, simplify hierarchy rather than merely removing necessary content.

claim: Test a layout without its styling and copy details; if the wireframe does not reveal a clear reading order, fix the structure before adding decoration.
why: Wireframing exposes whether clarity comes from genuine hierarchy rather than from ornament, imagery, or visual effects.
when: Reviewing a busy section or choosing between alternative layouts.

claim: Make the product category and value proposition prominent enough to be understood during a rapid scroll.
why: A small, peripheral product label can leave the overall visual message to imply the wrong type of brand or offering.
when: A hero or early page section is responsible for first impressions.
fails: The audience already knows the product context and the section has a different, narrowly defined job.

claim: Use real product UI imagery when demonstrating software, and subordinate decorative imagery so it supports rather than obscures the product message.
why: A dashboard screenshot makes the offering recognizable as software, while dominant lifestyle imagery can create a misleading impression.
when: Presenting SaaS, applications, or digital tools in a prominent marketing section.
fails: The product experience cannot be represented meaningfully by an interface screenshot, such as a primarily service-based offer.

claim: Avoid splitting a single message into many floating text fragments, pop-ups, ornamental details, and complex shapes unless each contributes to comprehension.
why: Fragmentation creates competing points of attention and makes a section feel crammed instead of deliberately composed.
when: A section contains multiple badges, callouts, decorative shapes, or independent text elements.
fails: The fragments form an intentionally ordered sequence and are visually grouped strongly enough to preserve a clear scan path.

claim: Establish a varied section layout in the wireframe before styling the site.
why: The early layout sets the direction for the visual character of the finished website.
when: Starting a desktop website or restructuring an existing page.

claim: Avoid repeating the same image-and-text two-column arrangement across consecutive sections.
why: Repeated column structures make a page feel predictable and visually boring.
when: A page contains multiple content sections with similar material.
fails: A deliberately uniform editorial, data-heavy, or system-driven layout is required.

claim: Introduce contrasting section formats—such as a full-bleed section, card group, and three-column block—to create rhythm.
why: Changing the spatial pattern of content makes the page feel more interesting.
when: Designing a marketing or brand-oriented desktop page with several sections.

claim: Introduce small, intentional overlaps between adjacent sections or components to reduce the rigid feel of an all-grid layout.
why: Overlapping breaks uninterrupted column-and-row alignment, making the composition feel more layered and engaging.
when: A page feels overly orderly, flat, or mechanically segmented despite having a sound grid.
fails: The overlap is large or poorly aligned enough to make hierarchy, spacing, or relationships unclear.

claim: Start box-breaking with modest vertical offsets across repeated cards rather than redesigning the whole layout.
why: Small staggered shifts suggest motion and visual rhythm while preserving the underlying component system.
when: Working with card-based sections that need more movement but must remain easy to scan.
fails: Offsets interfere with reading order, card alignment, or responsive wrapping.

claim: Allow selected content to extend past a container boundary to create depth and directional emphasis.
why: An element that crosses its frame visibly breaks the enclosing box and can make a section feel more dynamic.
when: A section benefits from a featured horizontal card strip, carousel-like composition, or deliberate edge tension.
fails: Overflow conceals important content, causes clipping, or looks accidental on smaller viewports.

claim: Keep box-breaking controlled, because overlap is easy to make visually awkward.
why: The technique trades structural regularity for energy, so inconsistent spacing and positioning can quickly look unintentional.
when: Applying offsets, overlap, or overflow within an otherwise orderly interface.

claim: Increase the size of the element you want users to notice first, rather than giving every element equal visual weight.
why: Larger elements naturally attract attention and create stronger hierarchy.
when: A page or section needs a clear focal point, such as a key statement, product feature, or callout.

claim: Vary scale intentionally across a page instead of relying on uniformly sized text and modules.
why: Differences in scale make the composition feel more visually interesting and less generic.
when: A layout feels flat, repetitive, or indistinguishable from a standard template.
fails: The variation obscures hierarchy or makes related content appear unrelated.

claim: Consider replacing a side-by-side two-column feature layout with a vertically stacked sequence when each feature deserves undivided attention.
why: A single-column progression limits simultaneous competing focal points and guides attention feature by feature.
when: Presenting a small set of important features, especially in a promotional or product-focused section.
fails: Users need to compare the two columns directly or scan dense information quickly.

claim: Establish one dominant focal point in a hero by centering key copy and increasing the prominence of the primary identity or headline.
why: The initial interface is functional but lacks a strong stylistic emphasis; concentrating attention on the name creates clearer hierarchy.
when: A portfolio or personal landing hero has several equally weighted elements and feels visually flat.
fails: The page needs left-aligned scanning, a secondary navigation pattern, or a different primary conversion target.

claim: Remove or shorten lower-priority content when it prevents the intended visual hierarchy from fitting comfortably in the viewport.
why: Reintroducing the statistics alongside the planned imagery created a vertical-space constraint, so surplus text was removed and content was moved upward.
when: A hero needs to accommodate meaningful visual work samples without becoming overcrowded above the fold.
fails: The removed copy contains required context, accessibility-critical information, or the page’s main conversion message.

claim: Use representative work imagery, such as device-screen crops, as the hero’s visual proof instead of relying only on decorative imagery.
why: Replacing the original image with several portfolio screens makes the portfolio immediately demonstrate the creator’s work.
when: The product or portfolio has attractive, legible visual outputs that can be shown at small scale.
fails: Screens are too detailed to read, do not represent the desired work, or create visual noise without curation.

claim: Animate related visual items with staggered entrance timing to make a static composition feel more engaging.
why: Staggered upward movement gives the screen collection a more deliberate and captivating reveal than showing all items at once.
when: A page-load or reload entrance animation supports a small set of independent visual elements.
fails: Motion delays access to content, ignores reduced-motion preferences, or is applied to dense or essential interface controls.

claim: Use shared column edges, aligned rows and semantic sections to replace redundant nested cards.
why: The alignment and grouping can preserve structure without layers of borders and radii.
when: A page has accumulated containers solely to organize its content.
fails: Retain a container when it communicates an independent group or interaction.

claim: Preserve grouping, recognizable controls and restrained default states when removing card wrappers.
why: Removing containers is useful only if the information remains scannable.
when: Flattening a card-heavy interface.
fails: A flat undifferentiated list loses the structure the cards supplied.
